#3436. Why Wiress From The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Looks So Familiar

This article contains spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping."

The original "Hunger Games" raised the stakes for Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson) by establishing that tributes from their home, District 12, have only ever won the Hunger Games twice in 74 years. That means they only have one mentor, the alcoholic Haymitch Abernathy (Woody Harrelson), unlike other Districts' tributes that have two mentors each.

"Hunger Games" author Suzanne Collins told the story of the first District 12 victor in "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes" — Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler), who won the 10th Hunger Games decades before Katniss was born and then vanished. Now, "Sunrise on the Reaping" tells how Haymitch won his own Hunger Games.

Haymitch was at a disadvantage before he even entered the arena, since there were no District 12 victors available to mentor him. To address this issue, the Capitol "borrowed" victors from other districts and assigned them to mention Haymitch and his fellow District 12 tributes. Those mentors are Mags Flanagan (Lili Taylor) and Wiress (Maya Hawke), younger versions of characters who first appeared in the second "Hunger Games" film/book, "Catching Fire."

Wiress (played by Amanda Plummer back in "Catching Fire") isn't in the movie much, but "Hunger Games" fans will likely recognize the actress playing her. The daughter of Ethan Hawke and Uma Thurman, Maya Hawke is one of the more charming "nepo babies" to come out of recent Hollywood.

Hawke has been acting in film and television since 2017, when she played Jo March in a BBC production of "Little Women." In 2019, she not only appeared in Quentin Tarantino's "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" as "Flower Child," a member of the Manson family; she also got her big break. Hawkey joined "Stranger Things" in its third season as Robin Buckley, working alongside Steve Harrington (Joe Keery) at mall ice cream store Scoops Ahoy.

The season seems to set up Robin and Steve as a new romantic couple ... until she reveals she's not into guys! Despite the show taking place in the 1980s, though, Steve is cool with it. While Season 3 of "Stranger Things" tends to be remembered as one of its weaker outings, Robin was a great addition to the ensemble and Hawke returned as part of the main cast for the subsequent two seasons.

Hawke has also worked alongside her father. In historical miniseries "The Good Lord Bird," where Ethan Hawke starred as radical abolitionist John Brown, Maya Hawke played Brown's daughter, Annie. When Ethan Hawke directed the Flannery O'Connor biopic "Wildcat" in 2023, he cast Maya as the famed author.

Maya Hawke's other film roles include parts in Wes Anderson's "Asteroid City," Pixar sequel "Inside Out 2" as the voice of Anxiety, and a part in the upcoming "Magic: The Gathering" film. Hawke is also a singer-songwriter and has released four studio albums ("Blush," "Moss," "Chaos Angel," and "Maitreya Corso") as of 2026.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is now in theaters.

#3433. Dustin Hoffman's Forgotten HBO Drama Series Was Canceled For A Tragic Reason

HBO launched on November 8, 1972, and has since produced some of the finest shows in television history. It has also produced plenty of swiftly forgotten and overlooked curios, many of which are actually quite good. The Dustin Hoffman-led "Luck" was, according to critics at least, one example. This horse racing drama looked set to be another ongoing hit for the network until it was canceled following the deaths of three horses involved in production, bringing a tragic end to the show despite the fact it had already been renewed.

David Milch began his career on "Hill Street Blues" before co-creating one of the best shows of the 1990s in "NYPD Blue." That alone would be enough to make him a TV legend, but Milch wasn't done. He managed to steer clear of the ill-advised "NYPD Blue" spin-off "Public Morals," which was canceled after one episode, but he did oversee his share of short-lived crime series in "Brooklyn South," "Total Security," and "Big Apple." It wasn't until 2004 that he struck gold again with the HBO series "Deadwood," arguably the best Western TV show ever made. After that, however, Milch's career involved creating little-known series that came and went without making much of an impact.

His 2006 series, "John from Cincinnati," was a strange affair that lasted just one season. "Luck," on the other hand, looked as though it could break the trend and go the distance. Set in the world of horse racing, the Hoffman-fronted series also benefited from the directorial talents of none other than Michael Mann, and became a critical hit, earning a second season renewal. But that second season never materialized after some unfortunate on-set events which forced HBO to cancel "Luck" despite the fact filming had already started on Season 2.

"Luck" was somewhat of a passion project for David Milch, who told the Los Angeles Times, "I've been thinking about doing a show like this for 25 years." The creator explained how his father had taken him to horse racing events since he was age five or six, and how he saw the horses as "heart-stopping beautiful." All of which just makes the story of "Luck" even more tragic.

Dustin Hoffman plays Chester "Ace" Bernstein, a gambler who after coming home after a three-year stay in federal prison immediately concocts a plan for revenge against those who helped put him away. His bodyguard, driver, and right hand man, Gus (Dennis Farina) acts as front for Ace's investment in race horse Pint of Plain. Meanwhile, Hoffman's gambler sets out to restore the failing Santa Anita racetrack as part of his plan for retribution. Nick Nolte also appears as a veteran trainer who now owns his own colt.

"Luck" premiered in January 2012 to positive reviews and looked as though it might have the potential to become one of the best HBO shows of all time. By the end of that month, the show had already earned a second season renewal. On January 31, 2012, the Los Angeles Times reported that HBO had ordered a further 10 episodes that were set to debut in January 2013, with production on the new season set to get underway in February. According to the outlet, the debut episode brought in 1.1 million viewers and the renewal was "hardly shocking" given Hoffman and Nolte's involvement. What was shocking, however, was that on March 14, 2012, the Los Angeles Times once again reported on the show, this time to announce it had been canceled altogether.

"Luck" Season 1 earned an 82% certified fresh rating on Rotten Tomatoes, with critics praising the cast and writing in particular. But behind all this success, there was trouble brewing. People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) had been on top of HBO and "Luck" since January 2012, the month in which the show debuted. According to The Hollywood Reporter, the organization had written to the channel to enquire as to the treatment of horses used in the show, and had followed up on numerous occasions thereafter.

As a report from PETA explains, two horses were euthanized during production of the first season. According to the group, "older, arthritic horses had been used in dangerous (and deadly) racing sequences" leading to the two euthanizations. What's more, the report cites "insiders at Santa Anita Race Track" as having provided information about a third horse that died on-set. Rather than push on, HBO pulled the plug and "Luck" was added to the expansive list of the best shows canceled after only one season.

A statement from HBO (via the LA Times), read, "It is with heartbreak that executive producers David Milch and Michael Mann together with HBO have decided to cease all future production on the series 'Luck.'" The network claimed to have maintained "the highest safety standards throughout production," but acknowledged that "accidents unfortunately happen and it is impossible to guarantee they won't in the future." "Luck" Season 1 continued to air, but production on Season 2 was brought to an end despite plenty of footage having already been shot. Today, Season 1 remains available on HBO Max.

#3431. Sorry, Vice City, but You’re the Most Boring Part of GTA 6

When Grand Theft Auto 6 was first announced, fans were thrilled at the prospect of returning to Vice City. The Miami-inspired location has always been one of the series’ most memorable locations, its neon-lit streets standing in contrast to the grittiness of Liberty City. While I was as excited as anyone to go clubbing and spend some time on the beach, after 70 hours, GTA 6 has struck me with one surprise thought: Vice City is the least interesting part of Leonida.

I don’t mean to say that Vice City sucks — far from it! It’s an immaculately designed video game city with more environmental diversity in any given corner than some open-world games fit into an entire map. The fact that it’s one of my least favorite places to spend time is more a testament to every other location in GTA 6’s Florida-inspired world. From small towns to the deep wilderness, every corner of Leonida is a delight to discover because every area feels so different.

I blame GTA 6’s opening chapter for spoiling me rotten. Jason and Lucia’s story begins in the Leonida Keys, a brilliantly constructed introductory area that I fell in love with instantly. As someone who is fascinated by the Florida Keys, the real islands that the location is based on, I was thrilled to find a digital space that so accurately captured a genuinely surreal part of America. The real Keys feel like an isolated nation, densely packing stores and suburbs onto narrow islands. The Leonida Keys feel both like an idyllic vacation hideaway and a mundane suburb, which gives GTA 6’s opening chapter such a distinct feel from the rest of the game. The small town nature of it makes for one of my favorite chunks of any GTA game.

Even after getting out of the Leonida Keys, it’s still a while before you get to Vice City. First, Jason and Lucia spend a stint upstate hopping around some small towns separated by vast farmland. Port Gellhorn has the feel of an industrial town, the kind of place that’s lined with used car lots. Some great action set pieces come out of that setup; one time I busted up a well-guarded abandoned bowling alley and wound up in a gritty gang shootout.

Way south of there, you’ll find Capri, another highlight. The squeaky-clean upper-class town is full of boutique clothing stores and high-end cafes. When Jason and Lucia arrive there, they are immediately profiled by street cops who clock them as poor outsiders who don’t belong in town. It stings considering how hard up for cash the two are when they get there, which turns the town itself into one of GTA 6’s greatest antagonists. Screw this place!

Even the stretches of map that seem empty at a glance are fascinating. Some of my favorite moments so far have been spent in Lummox County, which is largely made up of woods and mountains (despite IRL Florida not technically having those). Some of the best date spots and activities are up there, hidden alongside hiking trails. It’s also home to some true weirdos, like a group of “conservationist” gun nuts who say they are controlling the ecosystem by shooting at invasive lizards. Those weirdo discoveries make what could have been a dull, empty area into a place that I keep feeling compelled to bike around.

Between all of those areas, there are so many little pockets of the map to love. Hullet Marsh hides one of the game’s weirdest secrets amid the alligators. Tiny islands like Belpoint are quaint little escapes worth seeking out. Even unassuming stretches of road, like the area under Buckskin Swamp, will lead you to decaying mini-golf courses that make you feel like you’re in a state with a lot of history to it. I’ve seen every corner of the map, and very little of it has felt like a waste of exploration.

Vice City is excellent too, of course. It’s a perfect representation of Miami, right down to the hotel pools that I’ve sat by while visiting my brother, who lives there. Vice Beach is a highlight, and the various Keys around the city give the area a lot of diversity. It’s more just that I expected all of that. I know that Rockstar can get the hustle and bustle of cities right, because I’ve been playing GTA games since I was a kid. It’s more exciting to see GTA 6 branch out into more intimate towns and figure out how to make those just as exciting without the sports cars and nightclubs. GTA games have explored these spaces before, but the sheer mass of them here helps Leonida feel like a fully realized state with its own economic and political nuances from region to region.

My relationship to Vice City as it stands is similar to the relationship I have to Manhattan as a Brooklynite. It’s work island. Clock in, make some money, and leave the city limits at sunset to actually live a little. I’ll remember my mini-golf games more than the hours I spent sitting in traffic on Vice City’s freeways.

GTA 6 takes some liberties with its world around Vice City

#3430. A Classic Twilight Zone Episode Is Like A Sci-Fi Version Of An Agatha Christie Mystery

The second season of "The Twilight Zone" has some of the series' greatest twist endings, as the show proved unafraid to push into even more out-there science fiction and fantasy. One absolutely outrageous ending I haven't forgotten since childhood comes at the end of "The Twilight Zone" Season 2 Episode 28, "Will The Real Martian Please Stand Up?", written by series creator Rod Serling.

Somewhere in the rural United States, on a dark winter night, a UFO crashes out of the sky. Two state troopers investigate and track the missing pilot to a roadside diner, where a bus trip to Boston has stopped over for food and rest. The bus driver (William Kendis) remembers picking up six passengers, but there are seven in the diner — and he can't remember which of the six faces are the ones who boarded the bus with him.

"You've heard of trying to find a needle in a haystack? Well, stay with us now, and you'll be part of an investigating team whose mission is not to find that proverbial needle, no, their task is even harder. They've got to find a Martian in a diner," says Rod Serling in the episode's opening narration.

Writing about "The Twilight Zone" for /Film, Valerie Ettenhofer compared "Will The Real Martian Please Stand Up?" to an Agatha Christie novel. That comparison stands up quite sturdily. The episode is a closed circle mystery in the vein of "And Then There Were None" or "Murder on the Orient Express," complete with a twist ending that denies the simple answer of one suspect being the guilty person. But instead of looking for a murderer like Hercule Poirot would, the detectives are searching for an alien invader disguised as a human.

Like the best Agatha Christie mysteries, "Will The Real Martian Please Stand Up?" winds up the tension by trapping the characters together, because the bridge the bus was meant to cross is out of order. The winter setting complements this; cold weather amps up stress while forcing people to huddle together. Watching the episode decades later, it reads like an ancestor of John Carpenter's "The Thing" — both are about groups of people trapped in the cold and trying to find an alien hidden among them.

But unlike the many Agatha Christie books and movies out there, "Will The Real Martian Please Stand Up?" has to do the setup, mystery, and payoff in only 24 minutes. There's no "characters get picked off one by one" plot structure here, because with the episode's tight timeframe and seven suspects, there's just no way to do that. The episode still manages to capture escalating paranoia, like when even the two married couples among the bus passengers begin to suspect each other. The bug-eyed Mr. Avery (Jack Elam), who keeps laughing at the situation and prodding the others, is the obvious red herring in the ensemble.

There's also never any doubt the Martian is real and rejecting the pretense of ambiguity keeps the episode focused. There's physical proof in the footprints leading out of the pond where the UFO crashed to the diner, and as the episode goes on, inexplicable phenomena like lights flashing and sugar canisters exploding open plague the diner. Rod Serling's intro narration promises a real Martian, too. If this was all a misunderstanding, then it wouldn't be "The Twilight Zone."

The real Martian is the curt businessman Ross (John Hoyt), and you can spot an impressive amount of foreshadowing. Ross is one of three passengers traveling alone, leaving him without an alibi for his identity. (The POV panning shot when the troopers enter the diner shows him pointedly sitting alone. He also turns his head away as if trying to escape notice.) Avery jokes Ross is "the most suspicious of the bunch" and probably doesn't realize how right he was.

At the episode's denouement, the bridge is cleared and everyone departs without getting an answer. But then Ross saunters back into the diner, alone, telling the clerk Haley (Barney Phillips) that the bridge collapsed and everyone else died. That's when he reveals a third arm hidden underneath his coat, mixing his coffee as he explains his fellow Martians are coming to colonize Earth.

Rod Serling doesn't end on that semi-predictable note. Ross' reveal sequence includes close-up reaction shots of Haley, suggesting mounting terror as he finds himself alone with an alien invader. But then Haley agrees. "This is an extraordinary place to colonize. We folks on Venus had the same idea," taking off his cap to reveal a third eye. Haley was beneath both the audience and the troopers' suspicion — he wasn't on the bus, and he technically wasn't the Martian they were looking for, either. The ending avoids feeling like a cheat, too, because the whole mystery rests on there being an alien invader; if one of the diners is a Martian, is it that big a stretch that another is a Venusian?

The "Will The Real Martian Please Stand Up?" twist may not be more than a clever parlor trick, but what a trick it is.

#3429. Google Killed Its Dark Web Report, but You Can Still Monitor Data Breaches

Google’s Dark Web Report used to be the only consumer-focused platform that let users scan major data breaches, dark web marketplaces, and private forums to see if their personal information had ended up in the hands of hackers. But the company discontinued the service at the start of 2026, with new scans stopping on Jan. 15 and all accounts deleted on Feb. 16.

Google says it sunsetted Dark Web Report because, although the information it provided was generally useful, the service failed to provide “helpful next steps” for users whose data was found on the dark web. Google promised a new service that would provide more actionable intel, but that service has yet to materialize, and there haven’t been any further announcements about it yet.

Dark Web Report may not have been perfect, but it was the only early warning system of its kind that was available for personal use and let users run scans free of cost. Now that it’s gone, however, there are plenty of other services that offer the same service at varying costs and levels of effectiveness. Let’s talk through the nature of the insight that Google's reports offered, how it collected that information in the first place, and what options exist in the market to replace it.

Google launched the Dark Web Report in March 2023 as a premium feature available to Google One users, but later extended it for free to anyone with a Google account and moved it to the "Results about you" dashboard.

You'd set up a monitoring profile with your name, date of birth, physical address, phone number, emails, and Social Security Number if you lived in the U.S. After that, you could head to the dashboard anytime you wanted to run a free scan across dark web forums and marketplaces, publicly disclosed corporate data breaches, and other hidden online spaces to see if any of your personal information had shown up there. It was easy to use—but not a lot of people knew it existed in the first place.

It’s unclear what prompted the internal decision at Google, but in the absence of concrete next steps, it is reasonable to think the reports could create panic for the uninitiated. There’s no way to remove your information from the dark web once it’s already in circulation there. Still, having an early warning so you could reset 2FA or self-lock your SSN isn’t without merit.

But perhaps more importantly, most people with Google accounts didn’t know and hadn’t heard of the Dark Web Report’s existence. Google has likely taken it as a hint that users want more active remediation tools than simple alerts, which is why it’s now directing users to the Password Manager, Passkeys, and “Results about you” dashboard instead—though, again, the company hasn't followed through on a direct replacement for Dark Web Report, despite teasing such a feature.

Many of the top dark web scanners draw from the same well of information, scanning against major data breaches and dark web spaces. Several also offer breach notifications that send you email alerts when your details show up in a periodic scan. However, none of that is worth paying for because Have I Been Pwned or Mozilla Monitor cover those features quite well for free. Even the default password managers from Google and Apple come with some ability to monitor leaked credentials.

There isn’t an easy way to scrub your information from the dark web once it ends up getting leaked. But you can take steps to protect sensitive information or financial data once you know there’s been a leak. If a password has been compromised, reset it immediately. Also, enable 2FA on the affected account for added security. Even better, switch to a passkey if that account supports it. If not, authenticator apps are a safer way to receive 2FA codes than standard SMS.

If your Social Security number has been leaked, freeze your credit with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. You can do this by contacting each agency separately. Freezing your credit will prevent unauthorized credit withdrawals and protect your credit score from abuse by attackers. If one of your credit or debit card numbers has ended up in a breach, call your bank to freeze transactions on that card immediately.

Finally, get in the habit of using email aliases instead of sharing your actual email address with every platform and service provider. Addy.io and Proton’s SimpleLogin are both popular services that let you generate temporary email aliases that point to your inbox.

#3428. How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation

As soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing. It happens at a goodbye party for Raissa Molina (Liza Soberano), who is heading to Caltech. Her best friend Jo (H.E.R.) is late to the party and asks around to see where Raissa is, when an older woman points with her lips in the right direction. It’s a small moment, a visual gag that can easily go over the audience’s heads amidst all the other jokes in the sequence. But audiences familiar with Filipino culture immediately caught on to it, as did Latino fans and many others who recognize that gesture as the most potent and accurate way to point at something. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage

“That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire. “Growing up around Filipinos, the lip point was something that was so specific and unique to me, so it’s beautiful that it transcends into other cultures. Adding that felt like a celebration of it, but also something that makes characters feel real. And in adding that specificity about the culture, it ends up being the most universal aspect of the movie because it invites everyone in.”

The lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be important for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation. Later in the film, Jo does the lip pointing because an animator thought it would be a good idea to reprise it, after learning about its place in the culture. Indeed, in addition to having an authentically Filipino cast and a cultural consultant to really capture Filipino culture, the animation team found their own ways of homaging or capturing aspects of Filipino culture to bring to the movie.

When creating the character of Jo, the animation team based a lot of her hand expressions on Filipino skater Margie Didal and her own hand gestures, while the villainous Manananggal’s movements were created by the animation team watching choreography done by Filipino-American dancer Phil Tayag, who brought a pop locking influence to the vampire-like creature.

“When we first approached DreamWorks and Universal with this story, it was important to everybody that we got every detail of this story and this culture right,” director Januel Mercado said. “

After challenging what was thought possible with DreamWorks animated films in “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish,” Crawford and Mercado push the studio’s visuals forward with “Forgotten Island.” With most of the story taking place on the island of Nakali, which is populated by all sorts of mythical creatures, to really capture the fantastical possibilities of this world, the movie’s visuals go wild, taking inspiration from 1990s Filipino art as well as anime from that time period.

For Crawford, the big lesson learned from “The Last Wish” was that you could take big swings in the animation style and the visuals, but you could also do specific things in the story with those visuals. Indeed, when it came to “Forgotten Island,” the idea of memories and friendship became not only central to the story of Jo and Raissa, but also to the eclectic visual styles represented in the movie.

“The idea became that we could push the animation styles to represent the different ways people recall memories,” Crawford explained. “We didn’t need to be limited by Western CG-style animation, but actually bring in some of our own nostalgia into it and make sure it fit the characters. When Raww tries to explain what happened when he met Jo and Raissa, he sees himself as way cooler than he is, so he sees himself as Goku or Guile from ‘Street Fighter,’ the animation going 2D in an action-heavy tone. But when we meet Mermahn, he is very shallow and narcissistic, and we felt his glamorous point of view fit the aesthetic of ‘Sailor Moon’ with the silly kind of heart-shaped lens flare.”

Still, just because you can go Super Saiyan doesn’t mean you let go of reality. Instead, the directors worked with the head of cinematography, Scott Cullen, to make sure the film had a live-action look to it. The idea was to capture the nostalgia of growing up, while being able to feel the camera in the space the action takes place in, as if it was a physical set.

“Joel and I really wanted to make sure you feel like live-action, you feel the cameras there, and the way the light interacts with the lens is reminiscent of tangible photos we grew up taking, where you don’t know how they’ll develop,” Mercado said. “ We wanted to add imperfections, and to have interaction of weather on the camera, like condensation of rain and droplets on the camera.”

This all added to making “Forgotten Island” look like a part of the evolution of DreamWorks Animation, while standing out as something entirely fresh and unique. As Crawford said, the studio doesn’t really have a specific house style like other big studios. “Every movie requires innovation and pushing boundaries and finding solutions,” he added.

#3427. 5 Best Performances In The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping, Ranked

Major spoilers ahead for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping."

The newest movie in the "Hunger Games" franchise, subtitled "Sunrise on the Reaping," is here, and as I wrote in my review for /Film, it's a worthy addition to this genuinely excellent film series. Directed by Francis Lawrence, who has helmed every single Hunger Games movie except for the inaugural outing "The Hunger Games" in 2012 (which was directed by Gary Ross), "Sunrise on the Reaping" starss Joseph Zada as a younger version of Woody Harrelson's character, Haymitch Abernathy. Haymitch is one of the only known victors of the titular Games who hails from the downtrodden District 12 in the dystopian nation of as Panem. (Some housekeeping: District 12 is the mining district and impoverished enough that its child tributes for the Hunger Games almost never win; Panem is the redesigned totalitarian North America led by the oppressive Capitol, which is located in what we know as the Rocky Mountains.)

As Haymitch competes in the already-dangerous Hunger Games — made much more dangerous thanks to the fact that it's the second Quarter Quell, meaning it's an extra "special" (demented) version with double the child tributes — he encounters dozens of characters, some of whom we've met before in different timelines and some of whom are brand new. So which actors deliver the very best performances in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping?"

It's a stacked cast and it's legitimately tough to choose, but ultimately, I've picked five performers who build upon the previous movies and performances from storied actors who defined these roles originally ... and do so beautifully.

The only real beef I have with Elle Fanning's performance as Effie Trinket in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," such as it is, is that she doesn't get nearly enough screen time for my liking. Effie Trinket, who appears in this film as a sort of assistant stylist and District 12 prep team member who saves the sartorial day after her boss Magno Stift (Billy Porter) falls down on the job, is a character we know from the original "Hunger Games" movies; in those, she's played by Elizabeth Banks.

Effie is a larger-than-life character whose journey is, I'll be honest, sort of disjointed. When she's the chaperone for Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark (Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson) during the original stories alongside Woody Harrelson's grown, downtrodden Haymitch Abernathy, she seems slavishly devoted to the Capitol, but also becomes part of the rebellion in the two-part finale "Mockingjay." In "Sunrise on the Reaping," Effie seems to be a willing ally to Haymitch, but her loyalty still lies with the Capitol. (We also get to meet her younger sister Proserpina, played by Iris Apatow, for the first time in the series, expanding Effie's world just a little.)

Fanning, a recently minted Oscar and Emmy nominee for her sensational projects "Sentimental Value" and "Margo's Got Money Troubles," is unsurprisingly great during her unfortunately limited screen time, particularly her delivery of Effie's most memorable line from the novel ("I confess to having a moment!"). Honestly, there are so many prequels possible in the wider Hunger Games world, and if Suzanne Collins ever wanted to a deep dive on Effie's whole "deal" and give her her own story, I wouldn't hate that. But she'd need to convince Fanning to return to really make the movie sing.

I love Kieran Culkin, and I bristle when people accuse him of delivering the same performance over and over again. From where I'm sitting, that couldn't be further from the truth! Two of his most well-known and well-regarded performances — Roman Roy on "Succession" and Benji in "A Real Pain," the former of which earned him an Emmy and the latter of which earned him an Oscar — are very different. Roman is a broken man-child desperate for love that escapes him and that he does nothing to earn. Benji is a walking raw nerve, who is loved by complete strangers but is still desperately striving to make his own family accept him. Culkin's role in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" skews more towards Roman, but it's still a fun departure for the actor, and he's great.

Culkin plays TV host Caesar Flickerman. He's the second actor to play this specific character (Stanley Tucci originated the role in the original "Hunger Games" films) and the third actor to play a Flickerman TV presenter (Jason Schwartzman played Caesar's ancestor Lucky in the prequel "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes"). We know next to nothing about Caesar's psyche or inner life, and that's fine — he's just the guy who helps make a spectacle out of child murder. In any case, Culkin's bombast matches Tucci's wearier but still explosive host. When he's not snarling at assistants, he's Cheshire Cat-grinning at the doomed tributes. Across the board, he fits into this role perfectly. Culkin is not only a great casting choice, but a worthy addition to the franchise, and he delivers one of this prequel's best performances.

Ralph Fiennes is on what the kids might call a "generational run." In 2022, he played the sadistic and vengeful chef Julian Slowik in "The Menu," followed that up with a stunning performance as a troubled, grieving cardinal in "Conclave," and a two-film turn as the kindly and offbeat Dr. Ian Kelson in "28 Years Later" and "28 Years Later: The Bone Temple." Now, Fiennes has become the third actor in Hunger Games (and cinematic) history to play Panem President Coriolanus Snow. He follows Tom Blyth, who played a young and mostly unspoiled version of the future tyrant in "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," and the late, great Donald Sutherland, who portrays the oldest version of Snow that we see in the original films.

It shouldn't be news to anybody that Fiennes delivers an exceptional performance in "Sunrise on the Reaping." He is one of the finest actors of his generation and has consistently proven that across multiple decades. What was news to me, though, was how perfectly Fiennes bridged the gap between Blyth and Sutherland. Blyth's Snow begins his journey as a teenage boy desperate to prove his worth, and "Songbirds and Snakes" ends with him newly embittered by heartbreak and driven by ambition. Meanwhile, Sutherland's Snow is comfortable with being a source of pure evil and confident in his actions.

Fiennes' Snow sits beautifully in the middle as a man who seems like he still has an ounce or two of sympathy and regret left — he even asks Haymitch about the fate of Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler), the woman who loved and left him in "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" — but is still ruthless enough to replace a tribute tragically killed in a pre-Games accident with a brainwashed lookalike. He's excellent.

Without a perfectly cast Haymitch, the entirety of "Sunrise on the Reaping" fails. Woody Harrelson's Haymitch is deep in the throes of an alcohol addiction when we meet him in "The Hunger Games," and he's a disaffected, purposefully withdrawn man who clearly avoids getting close to District 12 tributes he views as doomed. Joseph Zada's Haymitch, in contrast, begins his journey as a young man with a lot to live for and a lot to love about his life. He loves his mother and younger brother and is besotted with his girlfriend Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak), a member of the Covey. Everything changes when Haymitch is randomly chosen to participate in the Games — he's not reaped, but chosen as a hasty replacement when the kid who was reaped makes a run for it and gets sniped in the head. Even then, Haymitch puts on a brave face, reassures his family, and even comforts the youngest District 12 tribute, Louella McCoy (Molly McCann), on their journey to the Capitol.

As Haymitch makes allies, forms a potential plan to blow up the arena alongside his mentor Beetee Latier (Kelvin Harrison Jr.) and Beetee's tribute son Ampert (Percy Daggs IV), and eventually allies with the other District 12 girl, Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), he suffers setback after setback. Zada manages to chart every single reaction and emotion we see from Haymitch in a way that feels real and earned. As he takes hit after hit in his quest to win the Games and return home — even though he'll only find more tragedy there — we feel every hit along with him. Zada is magnetic as Haymitch, and he's got a long career ahead of him thanks to this performance.

Every time I see a casting announcement involving Jesse Plemons, I'm excited. The dorky guy from "Friday Night Lights" — Mr. Kirsten Dunst himself — has become one of the entertainment industry's most reliably excellent actors. I'm struggling, as I write this, to think of a time where Plemons was actively bad in anything, and I'm coming up short. He can do absolutely anything, based on the fact that he's hysterically funny in "Game Night" and the most terrifying guy I've ever seen in "Civil War." I'm sure it was a daunting ask for Plemons to step into the role of Plutarch Heavensbee in "Sunrise on the Reaping" for one big and tragic reason: Philip Seymour Hoffman, who originated the role, passed away in 2014. I commend Plemons for taking the role, and I feel like I need to say that he bears a somewhat uncanny resemblance to the late Oscar winner (and even played Hoffman's son in 2012's "The Master"). He's also incredible.

Hindsight isn't always a gift for an actor, but in the case of Plutarch, Plemons clearly utilized everything we know about the character's future in "Sunrise on the Reaping." Plemons' Plutarch is a mere Capitol cameraman (Hoffman's Plutarch had been elevated all the way to Gamemaker), but he's shrewd, a favorite of Snow, and already a rebel ready to pursue a full takedown of the Capitol. Knowing that this comes to fruition across both parts of "Mockingjay" makes this look at Plutarch's early days of rebellion all the more satisfying, and Plemons is pitch-perfect as a man who's absolutely fascinating on the inside. It's the best performance in the movie.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is in theaters now.

#3426. Four Things You Can Do With Google Maps' New 'Ask Maps' Feature

Google has given its AI-powered "Ask Maps" feature a major upgrade, adding tools for trip planning, real-time route guidance, appointment finding, and saved-list search. The updates begin rolling out today on Android and iOS.

Google launched Ask Maps last March as an AI assistant designed to handle questions and requests more complicated than simply searching the word "bar" or "groceries." Instead of performing simple keyword searches, the idea behind Ask Maps is that you can describe several specific requirements at once, and Maps will find places that match them all. For example, you could ask for a restaurant with outdoor seating for a certain number of people, and "Ask Maps" will factor in your past searches and give you results. Of course, AI assistants have a habit of making things up, so even with today's roll-out, you'll want to double-check your sources before you drive an hour to the wrong restaurant.

To me, this is the most useful new feature launching today. Whether you're planning a day trip for holiday shopping or something more ambitious, like a three-day road trip with coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Ask Maps will put together a day-by-day schedule. Each plan includes insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop, so you can see the whole route at a glance. Once you're happy with the plan, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop.

When it's time to head out, you can ask Maps to pull up your itinerary, or look for the "itinerary" badge in your chat history. You'll see real-time details such as live traffic conditions, whether a place is currently open, and even the vibe at your next stop.

Plans can change on the fly, too. Ask Maps to add a scenic viewpoint or a lunch spot along the way, then tap to get directions to your next stop straight from the itinerary.

Here's what else you can use Ask Maps to do, starting today.

Pulling up directions now surfaces "Know Before You Go" tips for your route. These include where to park or charge your car, along with real-time conditions like weather, potential delays, and tolls.

Ask Maps is also gaining some agentic capabilities. Allegedly, you can just ask, “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me,” and Ask Maps will show you open slots across nearby businesses. In addition to finding appointments, Google says this agent will be able to call local businesses on your behalf—stay tuned while I wait for the upgrade and test this one out myself.

If you keep lists of saved places, Ask Maps can now search them for you. Ask something like, "Which spots saved in my lists have availability for 5 in the next 30 minutes?" Ask Maps looks across your lists and checks live availability, so you can pick a place and go.

These updates start rolling out today on Android and iOS. Travel itineraries and saved-list search are available everywhere Ask Maps is offered. "Know Before You Go" route tips and appointment finding are launching first in the U.S., with more regions coming soon.

#3425. 25 Years Later, Dragon Quest’s Island-Hopping Epic Gets Better in Every Port

The Dragon Quest franchise has been around for longer than some of us have been alive, and its first entry in 1986 was one of the JRPG genre’s pioneers. Over the years, the launch of a new title in the series has been a big deal, especially in Japan. Before players missed work to play Grand Theft Auto 6, they were using sick days to topple wicked dragonlords.

In North America, Dragon Warrior 7 (the last entry in the series to bear that localized title), arrived after two previous installments weren’t released outside Japan. Interest had waned. When the game hit stores on Nov. 1, 2001, it was as difficult to find as its NES predecessors had been. And when loyal fans finally tracked it down, we wound up being disappointed. But over the years, Square Enix has made some adjustments and tried again on multiple occasions. Happily, each new release of Dragon Quest 7 gets better than the one before it.

Dragon Quest 7 spent a long time in development and arrived late enough in the original PlayStation’s life cycle that it felt decidedly old-fashioned by the time any of us got the chance to play it. The visuals were a step above anything the Super Nintendo offered, finally rendered in 3D with a camera that players could rotate. But the experience still felt a bit like a step back compared to the flatter but more detailed environments of late PS1-era games like Final Fantasy 9. In some respects, it was a relic from a time many players had moved on from.

The quest’s opening hours didn’t correct that first impression. I remember playing for three hours without encountering a single enemy mob, which just felt odd. In the typical Dragon Quest game from years prior, you could head outside the castle walls within a few short minutes. An hour into the adventure, you would have already battled dozens or even hundreds of monsters and leveled up your characters several times. Instead, I had to spend that time solving tedious puzzles.

Slow opening hours eventually gave way to a lengthy quest with plenty of appeal, but I didn’t actually stick around to experience those later events until Dragon Quest 7: Fragments of the Forgotten Past launched on the 3DS on Sep. 16, 2016 in the West. Despite making its debut on portable hardware, the new release offered a superior way to experience the adventure.

The single change I appreciated most was an update to the formerly tedious first few hours of play. The introductory dungeon, with all of its levers and backtracking, was gone. Introductory areas still ate up more time than I was accustomed to, but they fit within a single gaming session and left me with time — and enthusiasm — to progress to more interesting activities.

The 3DS version offered other enhancements, as well. The bottom screen provided a helpful glow when the player approached stone tablet shards, a major component of progression. Players had a lot less guesswork to find essential items, a smart adjustment that eliminated a lot of pointless frustration.

Another new feature recapped the story, in case players stepped away for a few days, weeks, or longer. Accessible from the pause menu, a chronological log listed every major event that had occurred, along with hints about where to go next. (Later games in the series, all the way up to Dragon Quest 11, would keep this addition.) While exploring, party members might also offer suggestions if consulted, sparing players from some of the ambiguity that had been a franchise staple since its first installment.

Quality-of-life enhancements didn’t stop there, either. The game also introduced enemy mobs players could see in the field as they explored. Leveling up required less grinding, and menus were modified and streamlined. A map on the bottom screen made it easy to spot nearby points of interest. Most importantly, players could make a quick save outside of churches if they needed to stop playing suddenly. For a portable game, that option was a must.

Dragon Quest 7 on the 3DS remained the best way to play the game for a decade, until Dragon Quest 7 Reimagined launched in February 2026. Available on Switch, Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X, the updated take on the classic adventure introduced a breathtaking new art style. Presented like a diorama, the gorgeous visuals paired nicely with quality voice acting to bring the world’s story to life like never before.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

The newest release also introduced new changes to the character vocation system, allowing party members to adopt two vocations at once and gain mastery in both of them. Changing a class no longer required a time-consuming visit to Alltrades Abbey, either. And on the world map, striking weaker monsters defeated them automatically with lesser rewards, a welcome compromise that eliminated the need to endure tedious skirmishes. There were other changes, as well, including multiple difficulty presets, a shared inventory, and auto-revive after battle for party members who perished in the fight.

For RPG fans in 2026, these were smart adjustments. Few players appreciate busy work and random encounters that slow the pace more than necessary. It’s good to see developers revisiting past triumphs and modernizing them for contemporary audiences to enjoy. If at first you don’t succeed, try, try again. It certainly worked for Dragon Quest 7.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

As someone who has played the original DW7 at least 2 dozen times over the past 26 years (a few times with GameShark when I just wanted the story), I still love to go back to play those first few hours. As an 11 year old, that was the dream: going to the old part of the place you grew up in, and finding out it held a long-lost secret that only you and your friends can solve.

I wish that the original Ancient Fane and its puzzles could have returned, at least as an optional area. It set the tone for the game. This game wasn't going to be over soon, and if you could only afford one new game per year, you couldn't ask for more from this.

#3424. Jason Momoa Starred In A Gritty Western Thriller That's Streaming For Free

In 2014, Jason Momoa co-wrote, directed, produced, and starred in "Road to Paloma," a drama thriller designed to highlight the lack of justice for sexual abuse victims on Native American reservations. Momoa, who is of Native American descent on his mother's side, made his directorial debut with "Road to Paloma," which managed a sort of okay 54% on Rotten Tomatoes. Eight years later, he helped oversee another film centered on Native American heritage, this time in the form of a retelling of the legend of Willie Boy.

This "legend" is actually based on the true story of a member of the indigenous Chemehuevi people who fell in love with a woman named Carlotta in the early 20th Century. The pair absconded but were found and separated by their families. After Willie Boy moved to Banning, California, Carlota soon followed. But her father, William Mike, disapproved of the couple reuniting. He ended up dead, possibly due to having been intentionally shot by Willie Boy or as the result of an accident. After this began what's been called "the last Western Manhunt" in which Willie Boy was pursued by a Sheriff and his small posse over roughly 600 miles.

The story has since taken on a mythical status, and was adapted for the big screen with 1969's "​​Tell Them Willie Boy Is Here," which depicted events mostly from the perspective of Robert Redford's lawman. It was ultimately overshadowed by the actor's other Western from 1969: "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid." In 2022, however, Momoa, writer Thomas Pa'a Sibbett, and director Christian Camargo took another shot at adapting the same story in a very different way with "The Last Manhunt." If you'd like to see how it turned out, the film is currently streaming for free on Tubi.

Jason Momoa has a few underrated projects, but "The Last Manhunt" seemed more personal. According to Variety, the "Aquaman" star heard the story of Willie Boy while in the Joshua Tree area, where he owns a home. He and writer Thomas Pa'a Sibbett then developed the story, even meeting with direct descendants of Carlotta's family. The result was a version of the legend based on the Chemehuevi's oral tradition. As Sibbet told Variety, "This is a living story for the Chemehuevi people. It has a special place for them. So we can honor their oral traditions by just listening to them."

Momoa brought in Christian Camargo to direct, with whom he starred in the Apple TV series "See." Camargo previously wrote and directed 2013's "Days and Nights," which was based on Anton Chekhov's play "The Seagull" and boasted an impressive cast including Mark Rylance, William Hurt, and Ben Whishaw. Unfortunately, Camargo failed to do the Russian playwright's source material proud. "Days and Nights" currently sits at 0% on Rotten Tomatoes with critics ripping into the drama for having nothing to say.

All of which makes "The Last Manhunt" seem like an absolute triumph in comparison. The film stars Martin Sensmeier as Willie and Mainei Kinimaka as Carlotta, who trek across the desert after the death of Carlotta's father. They're pursued by Sheriff Wilson (Camargo) and a small group of indigenous people who want Willie to face justice for the killing. As the manhunt goes on, the ever more tragic consequences pile up. Momoa also appears in the film as Big Jim, a Native member of the posse. But he's only in a handful of scenes and isn't given much to do.

"The Last Manhunt" didn't make much of an impact upon its 2022 release. After debuting at the first ever Pioneertown International Film Festival, it received distribution by Saban Films. But its limited theatrical release in November 2022 came and went and the film has just sort of languished on digital platforms ever since.

Thankfully, it's now on Tubi and is worth a watch if you're a Western fan. A 20% Rotten Tomatoes score probably isn't the best selling point, however. Luke Y. Thompson of the AV Club gave "The Last Manhunt" credit for "great visuals and the best of intentions" but ultimately found it to be little more than "a basic posse movie" that's "not exciting enough to just do that well." Catey Sullivan of the Chicago Reader, on the other hand, praised the film for "reclaiming the narrative of a Native hero" and delivering a story that "is at once an epic romance and gripping thriller." There's also plenty of acting talent on display. Alongside Martin Sensmeier and Mainei Kinimaka as the leads and Jason Momoa's brief appearances, there's Lily Gladstone as Carlotta's mother Marie, Zahn McClarnon as her father, William Johnson, as well as Wade Williams and Raoul Max Trujillo as trackers in pursuit of the couple.

So, while "The Last Manhunt" is far from one of the best Westerns of the 21st Century, there's enough here for fans of the genre. Those interested to see whether Momoa and his cohorts managed to finally do justice to the Willie Boy legend should also find "The Last Manhunt" worthwhile. The film is available to stream on Tubi right now.

#3423. Curry Barker Would Have Completely Reshot ‘Obsession’ If He Could

It’s been quite a year for Curry Barker. In September 2025, he brought his $700,000 horror film to the Toronto International Film Festival, where it sparked a bidding war that Focus Features won for $17 million. That hefty price tag turned into the deal of the century, as “Obsession” went on to become a half-billion-dollar box-office sensation, with audiences growing week to week. It was clear the then 26-year-old “YouTuber” (a moniker Barker rightfully dismisses) was something special. This was not just a flash in the pan, but a real talent with a seemingly boundless number of ideas and movies he wanted to make. His next film, “Anything but Ghosts,” was already in the can by the “Obsession” premiere, a yet-to-be-announced third film is in the works, while potential franchises (“Texas Chainsaw Massacre” and “Obsession,” Barker sees the One Wish Willow story device having “Knives Out” anthology-like potential) linger in the background. Related Stories Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a New Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’ How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles

Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest new director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.

“I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really quickly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” said Barker on Toolkit. “I actually have no time to do those short films, and then justifying if it be would be worth my time to do them when I need to be writing this, I need to be editing this, and I need to be doing press for this.”

It’s less about Barker’s desire to scratch the itch of the shorts he never got to make, but more about a hesitancy to step away completely from the iterative process by which he learned his craft — justifying the brief time he took off to make “Mama Bear” because he felt the need to sketch.

“It’s fun to have that playground because the features are bigger stakes,” said Barker. “We were like, ‘Okay, this is a short film: We can do weird stuff. Let’s come up with crazy rules that don’t make sense, and experiment.’”

Barker and his “Mama Bear” cinematographer — his young brother Riley, who worked on the “Obsession” camera department — created different rules for the camera, as Curry is still trying to hone his discipline for storytelling within longer takes. Not only would they shoot a narrow 4:3 aspect ratio, but the Barker brothers denied themselves the ability to move the camera left, right, up, down, or dolly in.

“I do have a lot to learn,” said Barker of making “Mama Bear.” “It’s so funny because I was having dinner and I told someone, ‘Oh, I’d love to shadow on Ari Aster’s set.’ And someone was like, ‘Well, you’re Curry Barker, what are you going to shadow for?’”

His 2026 meteoric rise has allowed Barker to collect a group of more experienced peers he views as mentors — including Aster, Bill Hader, Zach Cregger, and Rian Johnson — and successful producers, like Jason Blum, investing in his career, but he believes there’s a misconception of what comes along with “making it.”

“People think that once you’re in this club, you’re in the club, and everyone talks to everyone. But no — you’re in a bubble, and I want to know how Zach Cregger writes his outline. I want to watch him do it,” said Barker. “You’re all alone. Your process is your own, and you figure this stuff out on your own. Once you get into this league, there’s no one telling you, ‘Well, actually you do it like this, this, and this.’ It’s whatever you learned all along your journey; that’s your process.”

One of the most impressive things about the self-taught Barker’s journey is how quickly he turned himself into a successful actor/writer/director/editor. In 2018, when Barker left Alabama to come to Los Angeles to pursue a career in movies, he saw himself as an actor. Despite all the story scenarios dancing around his head, the idea that he would become a screenwriter was laughable.

“I never would’ve thought I was a screenwriter. I didn’t make great grades. I made Cs and Ds, and I wasn’t the best in English class,” said Barker, who naively assumed professional writers were the kids who won spelling bees: “I just thought to be respected as a writer you have to be that.” Barker credits taking screenwriter Aaron Sorkin’s MasterClass as what opened his eyes. “It was the first time I thought, ‘I can do this, too.’ It’s really just about being creative and cracking a story, and there are rules, there’s structure.”

Directing organically grew out of Barker pulling together collaborators to shoot sketches and shorts for him to act in. Barker, half-joking, likes to say he realized one day that what he was doing was directing, and that he both enjoyed “telling people what to do” and had a knack for it.

What Barker accomplishes in a single shot — establishing a tonal balance that teeters between horror and comedy, combining blocking and camera movement to edit within the frame — is remarkably sophisticated. But Barker, who studies and strives for what masters like Kiyoshi Kurosawa can accomplish, quickly says he fell short in “Obsession.”

“Things that you might think we pulled off [with longer takes in ‘Obsession’], we reshot,” said Barker, who on the podcast described in detail a key early scene between Bear (Michael Johnston) and Nikki (Inde Navarrette) in the bedroom that had to be reshot because the action took too long to unfold. “I think Ari [Aster] said once that if you realize you needed to give this information in four seconds, but then it took 25 seconds, you’re stuck with 25 seconds.”

Curry Barker, the editor, is Curry Barker, the director’s harshest critic, giving him a bird’s-eye view of what he believes is the director’s inability to envision the required pacing of how a scene will play on screen, even if it might feel unnaturally fast on set.

“Every single oner that I’ve shot in my career has been a problem in the edit,” said Barker. “I think there’s two ways to fail at something. You can either fail, realize that it didn’t work, get scared of it, and then be like, ‘Well, in my last film I did a bunch of oners and then it killed me in the edit, so I’m not going to do that anymore.’ Or you can fail, realize how you did it wrong, and try to get better at that for the next time.”

As Barker discussed at the Future of Filmmaking Summit last month, that iterative process is key to how he got where he is, and it’s a mindset he clearly hasn’t given up. When asked how “Obsession” would have been different if he had more money, Barker doesn’t talk about locations, sets, special or visual effects, or scenes he envisioned that he couldn’t pull off — in terms of scale, he likes both writing and directing within set limitations.

“I would’ve reshot everything,” Barker answered without hesitation. “If I was finishing the edit before we got into TIFF, and you were like, ‘Dude, this is really good, we really love this movie, we think it has potential, but we want to give you $10 million to reshoot the whole thing, I would be like, ‘Deal.’ I would take it.”

“I think it’s so funny to look back and think about that now,” Barker catches himself, knowing he’s talking about a film that broke the box office and catapulted his career. “Now I wouldn’t change anything because I would be too scared to touch it.”

#3422. Before Slow Horses, Olivia Cooke Starred In One Of The Best-Reviewed Movies Of 2020

Apple TV's offbeat spy thriller "Slow Horses" just completed its sixth season this past October, and it won't be calling its quits anytime soon, having since been renewed for several more seasons. The vast majority of critics and fans believe the show hasn't lost a step (even with the departure of original head writer Will Smith at the end of Season 5), and its Mick Herron-penned source material still has meat on the bone. Thus, "Slow Horses" will likely run as long as Gary Oldman wants to keep chopping and literally stinking it up as Slough House chief Jackson Lamb.

The narrative arc of "Slow Horses" Season 6 was particularly gripping, as its team of misfit spies found themselves being unceremoniously liquidated. Lamb can't protect his operatives, so they're all forced to go into hiding. It's a perilous state of play for River Cartwright (Jack Lowden), the series' underdog protagonist who shows flashes of Lamb's spycraft expertise but can't quite put it all together. He needs help, and he receives it from seemingly beyond the grave when Olivia Cooke's agent Sidonie "Sid" Baker turns up in River's grandfather's house.

Sid was presumed dead in Season 1, but she's back in action in Season 6, and she throws a charge into the proceedings as the romantic spark between her and River threatens to burst into a white-hot flame. We should expect nothing less from Cooke because she's been superb throughout his career, and that extends to her crucial role in Darius Marder's 2020 critical darling "Sound of Metal."

In what might be her best work to date, Cooke stars in Darius Marder's Oscar-winning drama as a singer whose drummer boyfriend (Riz Ahmed) is dealing with rapidly encroaching deafness. Cooke could've easily been relegated to a stand-by-your-wounded-man role in "Sound of Metal," but she branches out and, via Marder and Abraham Marder's screenplay (and a story co-credited to Derek Cianfrance), locates the sadness in a woman trying to save the person she cares about more than virtually anyone else in the world. Unfortunately, as the film progresses, it becomes clear that her character no longer serves a function in her lover's life. It's a painful thing to watch, but they're on different journeys now, and while healing is entirely possible, they just can't heal together.

Cooke has never been better, but she's still one plum role away from transcendence. I can't wait to see how that plays out.

Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sharon Horgan had a string of British hits (including a couple we'll talk about here), before scoring stated successes with Divorce, Shining Vale, and Bad Sisters. She's quickly rising in the ranks of TV super-producers, the acerbically funny HBO Max rom-com Youth (in which she also stars) being just the latest.

This earlier series created by and starring Sharon Horgan is a family sitcom that feels far more believable than most, seeing Irish primary school teacher Sharon (Horgan) hooking up with American ad exec Rob (Rob Delaney) over the course of a week, only to discover that she's pregnant once he returns home. They don't really have feelings for each other, but decide to give it a go at being a couple, eventually falling into marriage just before the birth of their child. There are lots of jokes and plenty of acerbic dialogue, but this isn't Married... with Children. Sharon and Rob can be a bit nasty to each other and to their sloppy friend group, but there's also something rather sweet in the show's conviction that having someone to be a mess with can be one of life's great joys. Stream Catastrophe on Prime Video.

A little more of a high-concept here, but nevertheless an effective show about reimagining yourself in middle age. Younger follows Liza Miller (Sutton Foster), a recently divorced woman in her 40s who finds that age is a barrier to reentering the publishing industry she left years earlier. After a compliment convinces her that she could pass for a younger woman (poor thing), she manages to convince the right people that she's just 26 in order to land an entry-level job. Seven seasons of misadventures ensue, but much of the show revolves around the twisty-turny relationship between Liza and Josh (Nico Tortorella), a tattoo artist in his twenties. Stream Younger on Netflix.

Bridget Everett stars as Sam Miller, who struggles to find her new direction after moving back to her hometown to care for her dying sister. (Don't worry: There's plenty of comedy in the drama, and it's not as heavy as it sounds.) She's solidly middle-aged and starting over, kinda—making new friends in a familiar environment where she has to confront the past and the future alike. Luckily, her love of singing—and a community of goofy oddballs—are there to help. It's another story of a person of a certain age, trying to rebuild their life following an upheaval. Stream Somebody Somewhere on HBO Max.

When all else fails: Start a punk band. This drama from Sally Wainwright (Gentleman Jack) sees five women start a punk band as a lark, just a fun way to kill some time by entering a local talent context. The women realize very quickly, though, that they're very, very pissed off—about the workplace for women, menopause, a diminished dating pool, caring for aging parents and grown children—all of it tied up in the ways in which we treat women, and particularly middle-aged women. The band is a way to reclaim their voices, which doesn't erase or negate any of their problems nor drama (and there's plenty here), but gives them a platform with which to make some noise about it. Stream Riot Women on Britbox.

More of a traditional sitcom, not that there's anything wrong with that, this one builds a lot of goodwill with the performance of Leanne Morgan, its lead and co-creator (alongside Susan McMartin and Chuck Lorre). She plays the show's lead: a Knoxville, Tennessee wife and mom, who finds herself suddenly single in her 50s after her husband of 33 years leaves her. It's a genial, old-school hang-out show with a phenomenal veteran supporting cast that includes Kristen Johnston, Ryan Stiles, and Tim Daly. Stream Leanne on Netflix.

Michele Buteau, who also co-created the series) stars here as a fashion-forward stylist who'd devoted herself to the wrong guy for way too long. As the series opens, Mavis Beaumont is ready for a fresh start, putting herself and her career first—which does not preclude falling into a number of romantic entanglements. As she says more than once, she's going to take on the fashion world with a "body-positive attitude, cute v-neck, and some lip-gloss." Stream Survival of the Thickest on Netflix.

Certainly the goofiest take here on the idea of starting over in mid-life, this is very much a traditional three-camera sitcom, albeit one with a stacked cast of TV legends. Writer Melanie (Valerie Bertinelli), beautician Joy (Jane Leeves), and soap diva Victoria (Wendie Malick) wind up spending a wild night in Cleveland after a plane to Paris is diverted, discovering in the process that, while they're seen as over-the-hill back in Los Angeles, they're all Ohio 10s—though the sassy caretaker of their house, Elka (Betty White), might not agree. Stream Hot in Cleveland on Paramount+.

She'a s hair younger than Alex, but Fleabag (she's only ever referred to as "Fleabag") is trying to rebuild her life after a bad breakup, with extremely mixed results. This very dark comedy-drama follows a free-spirited, deeply angry single young woman living in London and sharing her romantic ups and downs via confessional asides to us, the audience. She falls, rather reluctantly, for "The Priest" (Andrew Scott)—while she's a confirmed atheist, and he's obviously not, the show doesn't turn aside from the general messiness of the situation. Phoebe Waller-Bridge won separate Emmys as the star, creator, and writer of the series. Stream Fleabag on Prime Video.

Maisel was one of Prime’s first truly buzzy original series, a comedy-drama from Amy Sherman-Palladino (Gilmore Girls) about the title’s Midge Maisel (Rachel Brosnahan), a long-time New York housewife of the late 1950s who discovers a talent for stand-up comedy. Inspired by the real-life careers of comedians like Totie Fields and Joan Rivers, the show is warm and welcoming, with great performances and dialogue; it also achieves something rare in being a show about comedy that’s actually funny. Stream The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel on Prime Video.

The big life change in this earlier Sharon Horgan hit is a little different: Julia Johnstone's mother had been a big help in taking care of Julia's children, but she's not going to do it anymore, leaving this working mom (Anna Maxwell Martin) to take the full brunt of childcare for the first time (her husband in the picture, but not much use). She joins up with other working moms involved with a local support group, including shallow Amanda (Lucy Punch), star of her own ongoing spin-off. Stream Motherland on Prime Video and Britbox.

#3420. Netflix’s (Very) R-Rated 45-Episode Sci-Fi Anthology Doesn’t Get the Attention It Deserves

A beautiful, ambitious showcase of animation as a medium

In 1981, the animated cult classic Heavy Metal fused hard rock and metal music with sci-fi and fantasy storytelling into an anthology film full of rich hand-drawn animation and rotoscoping from a dedicated team of animators. Some of these stories were adapted from Heavy Metal magazine, which has been publishing boundary-pushing genre tales with explicit content since 1977.

Almost four decades after the film’s release, filmmakers David Fincher and Tim Miller attempted to reboot Heavy Metal, which eventually morphed into the Netflix sci-fi anthology, Love, Death & Robots. Although the series inevitably carries the DNA of Heavy Metal and its contemporaries, Love, Death & Robots carves out its distinct identity over 45 exceptional episodes. While sci-fi is at the heart of these anthology tales, the show blends everything from horror to comedy to complement the bountiful art styles that are a celebration of animation as a medium.

Black Mirror may be Netflix's most famous sci-fi anthology, but if you're looking for something a little more hardcore, Love, Death & Robots is the perfect show for you.

Anthologies inevitably contain some middling episodes that miss the mark, and this is also the case with Love, Death & Robots. But the highs are so impressive that it's easy to overlook any episodes that are narratively shallow (despite still being gorgeously animated).

An example of an exceptional episode is “Zima Blue,” based on Alastair Reynolds’ acclaimed short story about an enigmatic artist named Zima who uses a specific shade of cyan blue in his artwork. While “Zima Blue” works with a surprising twist, the episode is about the existential search for purpose in life. It is also beautiful to look at, thanks to a clever mix of 2D and 3D animation that makes everything feel surreal.

Another standout is “Jibaro,” where a group of armored conquerors stumbles upon a bejeweled siren in a lake. Except for a deaf knight named Jibaro, all the men are driven into a violent frenzy after hearing the woman’s piercing scream. Jibaro approaches the woman, and the two are drawn together in a moment of intense attraction. Unfortunately, Jibaro’s greed overtakes any semblance of empathy, turning the episode into a metaphor for the violation that comes with colonialism. This 15-minute short uses hyperrealistic CGI with keyframe animation and motion-capture to evoke a jarring, dream-like quality that is worth revisiting.

The most interesting aspect of Love, Death & Robots lies in its explicit, no-holds-barred tone and subject matter. Explosive violence and casual nudity aside, the show doesn’t shy away from exploring humanity’s troubling tendency to play god, which informs our relationship with machines. Episodes like “Three Robots” and “Bad Traveling” focus on our moral failings, while “Sonnie’s Edge” and “Snow in the Desert” dissect a post-humanist landscape and the blurred lines between flesh and machinery. Love and obsession are also major themes, along with mortality, revenge, grief, and cosmic terror.

This wide scope of storytelling makes Love, Death & Robots feel fresh and inventive, even when the odd episode starts feeling like an exercise in style over substance. The show’s fourth volume proves how far it has come in terms of prioritizing quality over quantity, overcoming animation and storytelling challenges with smart, impressive short episodes. Some episodes, like “Spider Rose,” are follow-ups of previous stories, piling on unexpected themes and character conflicts that are refreshing to watch. The deaths are still gory and ultra-violent, but this artistic excess pays off in the end.

Love, Death & Robots has something for everyone. You can expect hard science fiction, war horror, nihilistic drama, and comedy to weave a perfectly bingeworthy series that takes pride in its stylistic animation. Live-action segments are also thrown in for good measure for those who seek variety. Not every episode is a hit, but when the show does make an impression, it leaves an indelible mark by setting higher standards for animated anthologies of a similar mold.

Love, Death & Robots can be streamed on Netflix.
