#3419. How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release “Minotaur” in theaters on Friday, November 20.]

World-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness. After contracting a severe case of COVID in 2021, he reacted badly to the Sputnik vaccine and was put into a medically induced coma for 14 days. When he came out of it, his arms and legs were paralyzed due to Guillain-Barré Syndrome. He lay flat on his back for a year.

When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair. While he says he hasn’t watched TV for 20 years now, “I watched a lot of films online,” he said through an interpreter on the roof of the Palais. “I read some things. I did not know if I would ever be able to walk again, to live again as a normal person. I have still now some consequences. I’m not at my best. I have regained completely the motion of my hands, but I have still a bit of a difficulty walking.” Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage

But he did manage to shoot his sixth feature film last year, but not in Russia. After nine months of waiting, in the spring of 2023, he let go of one expensive project (“Jupiter”) for which he couldn’t seem to raise funding. “I said, ‘Let’s put it on ice, we’ll come back to it later. I don’t want to sit and wait for years and years for you to find the money. I want to make a film now.'”

So instead the filmmaker focused on a parallel project he had also been developing, an adaptation of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” starring Stéphane Audran as a well-heeled wife cheating on her husband, which was later remade as “Unfaithful” with Richard Gere and Diane Lane. The result, “Minotaur,” is the “Leviathan” Oscar nominee’s first film in nearly a decade, since 2017’s “Loveless.”

At the same time that the filmmaker was coping with his illness, four years ago, at the start of the Ukraine war, he made the decision to leave Russia and move to Paris. Going home would mean the risk of being considered a traitor or an enemy of the state in Russia. “It might result in us becoming what is called foreign agents; it’s a hard thing,” he said. “Maybe this will happen, maybe not. Let’s not be too pessimistic, but mostly all independent journalists are saying that their oppressions are going to get even harsher, and that I think we have decades ahead of us before things get better.”

His 16-year-old had been studying at a French high school in Moscow before the war. “His French was pretty good,” said Zvyagintsev. “So it was an obvious choice. And also, my wife [has been] in love with France for a long time, she has been learning French for many years. So it was a choice, also for both of them, and for their future.”

How’s his French? “Zero,” he said. “The other reason for me was that France is the homeland to cinema; that’s where cinema was born, and also there are so many cinephiles among spectators. Also here in France, directors have the final cut. In the states, it’s much harder to get in a position where you are not censored; it’s not a producer or someone who decides instead of you.”

The filmmaker set about creating believable Russian locations in Riga, Latvia, which still resembles its neighbor country. “The dormitory suburbs around Riga look exactly like Russian dormitory suburbs,” said Zvyagintsev. “A Russian eye would not be able to distinguish between Russia and Latvia in this instance. As for interiors, Anton’s flat was constructed as a set, so it’s a constructed set, and the villa where the main characters live is a contemporary building, a very modern one, and you could find something exactly like this anywhere.”

When it came to finding his cast, the casting director put out a call for Russian characters of a certain age. “Every actor from anywhere who is interested in working with you, they will send you a video presentation,” said Zvyagintsev. “They can be from Argentina, London, Moscow, Paris, wherever. You send them a scene they have to play, and they make a self-tape for you on their iPhone. Before, I despised self-tapes, but it’s convenient, because now with everybody scattered around the world, it’s the only way for us to work. We could not possibly pay for all the people I wanted to check to come to Riga to make a real-life casting. There were people also from Riga who do speak Russian.”

One serious issue for Russian actors still living in Russia was the possible repercussions of participating in a Zvyagintsev project. “I would talk to them about the script and show them parts of the script, so that they know what they’re getting involved in, because, of course, they were at risk of getting blacklisted,” he said. “Most of them, with heartache, refused to take part in the film, but there was one who accepted, and I’m still completely amazed at his courage. It’s the main part, the main character, [actor] Dmitriy Mazurov. I said to him, ‘Are you sure you want to film with me?’ And he said, ‘If I’m not doing this part, I don’t know what I’m doing in acting.'”

Of course, the filmmaker took a different approach to the Chabrol story. “In the first minute, the story is completely revealed,” he said. “We understand that she is being unfaithful, so then all the film is about observing him, observing her, trying to understand, hesitating, and trying to guess what is going on, and while he observes, the spectator starts doing it along with him. And after the murder, actually, he goes back to this position where he’s mostly observing her reaction to the disappearance of a lover, yeah, and she knows what’s going on, and again it’s about observation.”

The filmmaker loved one bravura sequence that is 20 minutes long without any dialogue at all. “The sequence after the murder, it’s 20 minutes, even a little bit more, with not one subtitle, so you only observe his actions, and there are no words: it’s extremely cinematic in its essence.”

And Zvyagintsev added many telling details from the real world, from corruption to the war. “The Chabrol film is much more classical,” he said. “It follows a pattern: he killed, then he’s discovered, and then he will be punished. And I wanted to break up this classical structure and to invent something different based on our Russian realities.”

Was shooting the movie a physical challenge? “When you are full of inspiration, when you are searching constantly for solutions, the light, the sets, the performance of the actors, you don’t feel fatigued in the same way,” he said. “There is such a joy in making the film that is, in your head, real. I think it’s the best drug there is.”

Next up, he will try and resuscitate “Jupiter.” ” I have met some producers who are interested in it,” he said, “so hopefully we will be able to get it moving again.”

#3418. 5 Actors Who Should Play Felix Leiter In Robert Pattinson's James Bond Movies

Amazon MGM is shaking things up with their upcoming James Bond movie, and why the heck not? The end of Daniel Craig's Bond tenure in "No Time To Die" left the franchise in a sorry state of affairs and it's time to rejuvenate the saga with some fresh blood and new ideas. Robert Pattinson's casting as Bond suggests things are on the right track. The British actor is the first major star to debut in the tux, breaking more than 60 years of tradition and suggesting Amazon and director Denis Villeneuve are ready to try new things.

For now, however, we're yet to learn who will surround this A-list Bond. The supporting cast provides yet more opportunity to refresh the series, and while he might not be as crucial to the 007 formula as, say, the Bond girls or M, Felix Leiter presents a particularly exciting opportunity in that regard.

The character, first introduced in the inaugural Bond novel, "Casino Royale" in 1953, has traditionally been a CIA agent and Bond ally. Since the first 007 movie, 1962's "Dr. No," we've seen various iterations of Felix and multiple actors in the role. Some have been older and avuncular, some have been younger American 007 counterparts, and some have been boring bureaucrats. But for the most part, the character of Felix Leiter is yet to be fully explored. As such, the upcoming "Bond 26" presents a chance to do something completely new with Felix, and we think we have the actors for the job.

In 2017, James Bond's greatest ally got his first solo mission in comic books. The "Felix Leiter" comic book mini-series, from writer James Robinson and illustrator Aaron Campbell, gave the titular CIA agent his own story and missions separate from his British counterpart. The story saw him leave the foreign intelligence service and become a private detective, but that's beside the point in this instance. What could be really interesting is if Amazon MGM uses "Bond 26" to introduce a version of the character who could similarly carry his own on-screen spin-off. Aaron Pierre would be perfect for the job.

Pierre is fresh off a great performance in HBO's "Lanterns" and previously delivered a memorable turn in Jeremy Saulnier's gripping 2024 actioner "Rebel Ridge." As such, he's proved he has leading man chops. "Lanterns" also saw him convincingly play an ex-Marine, which just so happens to be part of Felix's background — at least in the books. With DC Studios now reportedly being dismantled by real-life Bond villain David Ellison, Pierre might be looking for a job and Amazon MGM should give him one.

Why not turn Felix into an action hero of his own? Everyone is surely expecting Bond spin-offs now that Amazon owns the IP, and as the comic book series proved, Felix is an ideal candidate. Of course, the character can't overshadow Bond in the upcoming film, but that doesn't mean you can't build him up over time to be a worthy competitor to Robert Pattinson's MI6 sleuth. Whether he remains a staunch Bond ally or there's some competition between the two it would make for a fresh dynamic in keeping with Amazon and Denis Villeneuve's new direction for the franchise.

Everybody knows that Jack Lowden almost became the new face of the James Bond movies, before missing out on the lead role to Robert Pattinson. The "Slow Horses" star would have made an excellent 007 and regardless of how exciting it is to have Pattinson in the tux, it's also a shame we won't see what Lowden would have done with the part. But that doesn't mean he can't play another role in Amazon MGM's new Bond-verse, and Felix Leiter seems like an interesting option.

It could, I suppose, be seen as a bit of an insult to hand a Bond hopeful a supporting role. But it shouldn't, given the aforementioned potential for spin-offs and exploring Felix Leiter's character more extensively. Things could get really interesting if Denis Villeneuve and "Bond 26" writer Steven Knight made Felix into more of a rival to Bond. With Lowden and Pattinson's Bond audition history, there's a built-in tension there already. If Lowden were to play an American Bond counterpart who clashes with Pattinson's agent, that would be a hugely compelling on-screen rivalry to watch play out.

Yes, Felix has historically been a Bond ally. But with the franchise entering a new era why not switch things up? Have Lowden play a version of Felix who gives Bond a run for his money. Capitalize on the Pattinson/Lowden audition history and watch the dollars roll in. With "Slow Horses" being as good as it is, it only feels right to bring Lowden into the fold in some capacity and this could be a really interesting way to do so.

If you haven't seen "Lioness" you might be wondering who this dashing stud of a man is. Well let me tell you. Thad Luckinbill is one of the most charismatic, endlessly watchable actors in Taylor Sheridan's spy thriller series. As CIA senior case officer and all round hardman Kyle McManus, Luckinbill brings a mix of smarmy charm and ruthlessness, deadly efficiency that would make for an exciting compliment to Robert Pattinson's Bond.

Kyle is, in many ways, the opposite of 007. He's loud, brash, and outspoken. But he shares much in common with Bond in that they're both supremely confident and solipsistic. If Luckinbill could bring some of that Kyle energy to Felix Leiter, the character could become either a wonderful foil to Pattinson's more urbane spy, or perhaps even pose a bit of a threat.

When he first appeared in "Casino Royale" back in 1953, Felix Leiter was a former Marine working for NATO's Joint Intelligence Staff who allied with Bond. He and 007's connection was a way to represent the United Kingdom and United States' "special relationship." With Pattinson so easily exuding the public school boy aura of Bond (it's one of the reasons he could be the best Bond yet) and Luckinbill effortlessly encapsulating the more traditionally brash American approach, these two side-by-side could make for a brilliant Trump-era representation of the somewhat strained yet still resilient "special relationship."

"Tenet" was full of confusing moments, to the extent that the entire thing was arguably one big confusing moment. What wasn't in doubt, however, was the fact that Robert Pattinson and John David Washington had chemistry.

Fittingly, Washington played a CIA agent known only as The Protagonist in Christopher Nolan's confounding thriller, alongside Pattinson as his handler, Neil. Together, they were an American and British spy team who brought very different energies to their roles. Neil was quite prepared to blow a freeport sky high, while Washington's Protagonist remained wary, making for a fun dynamic between the pair. Neil always seemed to be one step ahead and ready to do whatever was needed to get the job done, while The Protagonist remained constantly surprised by his cohort's knowledge and boldness.

If Washington is cast as Felix Leiter in "Bond 26," we could see a similar dynamic between the pair, which wouldn't be the worst thing in the world — especially if it were given more space to develop outside of Nolan's narrative machinations. Or, we could see a reversal of the dynamic, whereby Felix is even more of a daredevil rogue than Bond. Either way, the duo have proved their on-screen chemistry and would make a great Bond/Felix pairing.

You can chart Robert Pattinson's transformation from teen heartthrob to versatile character actor mostly via his portrayal of freaky little weirdos. The man just has a knack for playing off-kilter and slightly creepy types. But he's far from the only actor in Hollywood who seems to have that dark, subversive energy simmering below a relatively calm exterior.

Jesse Plemons is arguably just as exciting an actor as Pattinson. He's been consistently delivering compelling performances over the last decade or so and while his particular energy might work well as a villain, it could also be really interesting to see him working with, or at least alongside, Pattinson's James Bond. Both actors are capable of fully inhabiting their characters and simply seeing them bounce off of one another would surely make for some of the most interesting scenes in "Bond 26." Or, Plemons could bring the same "Civil War" energy that previously made his co-star cry to the role and give Bond a real run for his money.

Casting an actor of Plemons' talents in the role also allows the producers to really lean into a Felix spin-off in the future. Plemons has the chops to make a character study of Bond's favorite ally work, and I for one would watch the heck out of a Plemons-led Felix Leiter miniseries. Otherwise, the actor is yet to play a character like Felix, and it would be an interesting change of pace for him.

#3417. You Can Try WhatsApp's New Disappearing Text Messages Early

Like Snapchat messages, WhatsApp's "View Once" feature is a great way to send things you don't want living on your friends' devices. You can send voice messages, photos, and videos that will "self-destruct" after they're opened, limiting (if not eliminating) the risk of your friends keeping them forever. However, View Once has a major limitation: While WhatsApp will let you send voice memos and images that way, you can't use it to send texts, meaning every one you send will live on (unless you unsend it yourself).

That's now changing. As reported by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is now beta testing View Once for text messages, too. Soon enough, you'll be able to send voice memos, photos, videos, and texts as one-time-only messages. That way, you can send sensitive information via text—say, a password or an important account number—without worrying about it persisting. Here's how it works: You craft your text message as you usually do, but rather than tap the send button, you hold it. You'll see the usual "Schedule message" option, but once the feature rolls out, you'll also find a new "View Once" option as well.

As mentioned above, this feature is currently in testing, so it's only available to WhatsApp beta testers. What's more, only the Android version of the beta has access at the moment, so iOS beta testers are out of luck. (That said, the WhatsApp iOS beta is perpetually full, so there's not much you could do even if WhatsApp made this test available on iPhone.)

If you have an Android device, you can enroll in the WhatsApp beta to try out "View Once" text messages today. According to WABetaInfo, the feature is live as of WhatsApp version 2.26.45.6. To enroll, open the WhatsApp beta page on the Google Play store and enroll your account in the beta. If you don't have WhatsApp on your phone already, download it here; if you do, reload the page and install the latest update. This will update your existing WhatsApp app to the latest beta version.

#3416. Marvel’s New X-Men And Fantastic Four Reboots Have Already Made One Major Mistake

Marvel’s Midnight universe only has a few books out right now—Midnight Fantastic Four, Midnight Spider-Man, and Midnight X-Men—and only one of them has made good on the publishing line’s core premise as being horror-centric. These are all stories reinterpreting or retconning traditional Marvel Comics lore, of course, but the promise alone of uniquely scary or ominous retellings was the hook that they were all supposedly going to abide by, and there’s an argument to be made that Midnight Spider-Man is far scarier than Midnight Fantastic Four and Midnight X-Men, with it not being a close race in the slightest.

Of course, these books have barely taken off, and it’s likely that genuine horrors are in store throughout the next couple of years. Indeed, Midnight Fantastic Four and Midnight X-Men have spent a lot more time on worldbuilding, and their payoffs could be extraordinary. That said, issues of Midnight Fantastic Four and Midnight X-Men also aren’t taking advantage of one of their greatest horror tools, whereas Midnight Spider-Man is: Marvel Comics’ cloaked covers.

It’s disappointing that Midnight Fantastic Four and Midnight X-Men haven’t dove fully into horror because the Midnight publishing line is deliberately meant to be a horror-centric continuity. It may be unrealistic to expect that every single issue will have something scary in it, but Midnight Spider-Man has successfully achieved that in the two issues that have been released thus far. Ultimately, it seems to boil down to the fact that Midnight Fantastic Four is more of a sci-fi mystery story, and Midnight X-Men is more of a fantasy love story. Still, it’s jarring that Midnight Spider-Man leans wholly into horror while the others don’t, or haven’t.

Even odder is that Midnight X-Men is specifically rooted in Earth-616 X-Men lore and history, while Midnight Fantastic Four and Midnight Spider-Man are completely distinct. Midnight X-Men’s holy war between mutantkind, vampires, and empyres has the makings of a phenomenal story, especially given how Cyclops and Jean Grey’s relationship has evolved via issue #2, but it’s difficult to argue that it’s a horror story. Likewise, Midnight Fantastic Four’s cosmic horror has laid foundations for a particularly atmospheric and eerie dread, though there hasn’t been anything particularly frightening about the series yet. Meanwhile, Midnight Spider-Man wasted no time delving into gruesome body horror.

Issue covers have the potential to illustrate how horrifying these books can be, and cloaked covers further emphasize how much scarier Midnight Spider-Man is than Midnight Fantastic Four and Midnight X-Men. Midnight books cloak their main covers in order to obscure or mask the full artwork, “only revealing themselves to readers daring enough to pick them up on stands,” as per Marvel, but Midnight Spider-Man is unsurprisingly the only one to truly capitalize on the shock and awe that the presentation of the cloaked covers permits them.

For instance, the main, cloaked cover for issue #2 merely depicts Midnight Spider-Man’s Felicia Hardy in a state of fear, and it’s teased that something lurks behind her. The revealed cover shows that she’s right to be afraid, as Peter Parker’s terrifying Spider-Man is creepily nestled into the corner of the ceiling. Neither Midnight Fantastic Four nor Midnight X-Men has any such reveals yet, at least none that are anywhere near as scary, or that utilize the format as well.

Plus, Midnight Fantastic Four awkwardly always needs Reed Richards, Sue Storm, Johnny Storm, and Ben Grimm to be positioned vertically so that they can all be seen in this cloaked format, and X-Men’s massive ensemble has the same problem. Chiefly, it seems to boil down to Midnight Spider-Man being scarier and having the horror legs to stand on. That doesn’t mean Midnight Fantastic Four and Midnight X-Men are lesser, but it’s weird that they aren’t indulging in horror as much as they could be.

Midnight Spider-Man #3, Midnight X-Men #3, and Midnight Fantastic Four #3 are scheduled to be released on December 16, 2026.

#3415. GTA 6 Is Getting Review Bombed in Zelda vs. GTA Troll War

Soulcalibur catches strays in Metacritic feud

Grand Theft Auto 6 may be the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic, and may have earned a record-breaking $3.79 billion on launch day, but that doesn't mean Rockstar Games' new blockbuster can't have its haters. Multiple groups have descended on GTA 6's Metacritic page to attack the game for its perceived shortcomings, much of that criticism is based on culture war nonsense.

But some of GTA 6's detractors are targeting the game for another reason: for slighting The Legend of Zelda.

GTA 6 made its debut on Metacritic with a 99 Metascore, based on more than 150 critics reviews. That feat nudged the previous best game of all time, at least going by Metacritic score averages, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, down to No. 2 on the review aggregator website. That has led some Legend of Zelda supporters to review bomb Grand Theft Auto 6 on Metacritic, and some GTA 6 supporters to do the same to Zelda. Now, both camps are in a pointless war to lower the other franchise's user review score.

Over the past few days, GTA and Zelda fans have been trading barbs and slinging "0" user review scores at their perceived rivals. As of Sunday, Nov. 22, Grand Theft Auto 6's user review score on Metacritic has dipped to 5.6, indicating "mixed or average" reviews from players. In response, the original Ocarina of Time and its Nintendo Switch 2 remake have also been review bombed (though their user scores are in the mid-8s as of Sunday).

Unsurprisingly, the discourse around this pointless feud has not been particularly intelligent. Each camp is simply trying to drive down its rivals’ user score, with supporters writing the bare minimum in their user "reviews" — often with plenty of typos.

Even poor Soulcalibur, the 1999 fighting game released on Dreamcast, is catching strays amid the fighting. Some GTA 6 supporters are now wading into Soulcalibur's user reviews, slamming Bandai Namco's weapons-based fighter for no good reason beyond its ranking as the third-best game of all time according to Metacritic's algorithm.

Grand Theft Auto 6's detractors aren't just misguided Zelda fans. Unsurprisingly, a contingent of GTA fans are attacking the game for its perceived "wokeness" amid more legitimate concerns about performance. "30 FPS, Concole Exclusive, Restricted freedom and uninteresting characters are a no go for a 13 year development cycle," reads one recent negative review of GTA 6. Much of the feedback, however, seems to focus on having a female co-lead character and game mechanics that ask players to be considerate toward her.

"In GTA6 you need to do chores, pick up an abusive girl from prison and then do more chores. Boring characters, boring missions and 30fps cap. I would have rather burned that $100 than giving it to the woke garbage R* has become," reads one scathing review.

"15 years for this dissapointing cuck simulator. Rip rockstar. You were my childhood," reads another. "Game is straight woke trash," another troll says.

The tenor of GTA 6's negative reviews isn't much different from the trollish feedback infesting reviews of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, surprisingly. "THEY MADE LINK A CUCK IN THIS GAME!!!!! ALWAYS DOING WHAT HIS FEMALE FAIRY NAVI TELLS HIM WHAT TO DO!!!! CRITICS PROVE ONCE AGAIN THEY’VE BEEN BOUGHT OFF!!!!!" reads one of the many negative reviews to invoke cuck simulator language.

While this kind of petty squabbling is par for the course in internet discourse, especially in the video game sphere, at least fans of both The Legend of Zelda and Grand Theft Auto can take comfort in knowing that both franchises have great games to enjoy in 2026. And that, if you're reading this, you're likely not spending your time fighting in the Metacritic comments.

#3414. I Tested Pangram to See If It Can Really Detect AI-Generated Content Like It Claims

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

We know it can be difficult for human beings to spot AI-generated content, but can detection software fare any better? Pangram is one of the leaders in the field, promising a "near-zero false positive rate" by looking at "subtle cues" in the writing, based on a training and feedback model comparing human-made content with the AI equivalent.

You'll find arguments on both sides of the debate as to whether or not Pangram's claims stand up. After a short story was flagged by Pangram and then judged to be free from AI, the detection engine has been accused of bias against text from minority writers.

Proponents of Pangram would point to an ongoing reward offer—currently at $3,950—available to anyone who can find a pre-2019 (and pre-LLM) piece of writing that Pangram falsely flags as being AI-written. So far, the reward is unclaimed.

As the AI detector has recently added AI image and video detection to its capabilities, it seemed a good time to put Pangram's analysis skills to the test for myself. Here's how it performed in the three different content types.

On the human side, I picked out 10 of my most recent articles for Lifehacker, known to be written by a person because I personally wrote them—in the traditional way, I fretted over word choices, went back and changed sentences, and accidentally left in a variety of typos that editors thankfully fixed.

For the AI content, I rotated between ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, and got the LLMs to write 10 articles with the same headlines and the same approximate number of words, for a tech-savvy audience. I even asked the AI apps to vary their language use, so that the output would "read less like an LLM has written it."

Pangram's AI text detector lets you upload files, but to make the task a little harder, I copied and pasted all of the text into the online article, so it wouldn't be able to rely on any metadata included in the file. The scans got the correct result each and every time: Human-written text came back as 100% human, and AI-written text came back as 100% AI.

What's more, Pangram was certain about its results. All of the human writing was marked as highly likely to be human, and the vast majority of the AI writing was marked as highly likely to have come from an LLM. There were only a handful of phrases or sentences across thousands of AI words that got a "medium" rather than a "high" ranking for AI.

Now, there have been some edge cases where Pangram has got it wrong—like a poem repeating the same six words thousands of times—but as far as this sample goes, it can't be faulted. Clearly, my writing is too idiosyncratic and too clunky to be confused for the smooth sheen of AI-produced prose.

To be fair, I do have another advantage over AI: I can actually test out devices and apps in a way that LLM bots can't. ChatGPT can't experiment with One UI 9 (at least not yet), though it can scrape the web for various experiments and tests that real people have done.

However, I was able to fool Pangram to some extent by alternating AI paragraphs with human-written paragraphs. The text was flagged as AI, but the percentage estimate was typically lower (20-25%) than what it actually was (around 50%). If you're offloading some but not all of your writing to AI, some of it might slip though as real.

Image and video detection is the new string to Pangram's bow, so I sifted through my phone's photo and video library for some pieces of content to test the AI on. Again, I used copy and paste to get the files into Pangram rather than uploading them, to limit how much information the AI detector could get from metadata.

Again, all the human-made content was recognized as such, with a very high level of certainty—whether it was complicated crowd shots or simpler images of natural scenes. Presumably, there are even more signals to go off than there are with writing, including camera movements, colors, style, consistency, and composition.

Next up, I generated a few images and videos in Google Gemini and ChatGPT, requesting results that would look as photorealistic and "non-AI" as possible—the resulting files covered people, animals, and buildings. As before, I used copy, paste, and a few screengrabs to try and limit the metadata Pangram had access to.

Here, too, the AI identification was spot on, with all of the artificial content recognized as such, to a high level of confidence. This is perhaps not surprising: I think AI images and especially AI video still have more "tells" than AI writing, especially if you've seen a lot of it, so I wasn't expecting Pangram to fail here.

I did try experimenting with real photos that had a little bit of AI in them, what with tools like Gemini and ChatGPT now so good at image editing, as well as creating pictures from scratch. These were marked as "unsure" by Pangram, though to cut it some slack, only a small amount of the images were altered.

As with the text, the best way to beat Pangram's detection systems seems to be to include some AI embedded in human-made content. It will most likely still fail the "100% human" test, but the tests I ran showed that Pangram is less certain in these cases, or underestimates the amount of AI there actually is.

Increase the level of AI, and the detection gets more reliable—but if you're only using AI for a small part of whatever it is you're making, it's less worthwhile using AI tools anyway. As far as these tests go, Pangram's claims about accuracy check out, making it a useful tool if you need to ensure something is AI-free.

#3413. ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch

Even six decades into his Hollywood career, Steven Spielberg is still synonymous with a brand of movie magic and spectacle that very few can rival. And when he decides to direct a new popcorn blockbuster like “Disclosure Day,” you know you’re in for a few dazzling sequences.

One of the most exciting moments in the film comes when a train collides into a car with stars Josh O’Connor and Emily Blunt close at hand. The sequence tested every department, from camera and production design to visual effects. And during IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, VFX Supervisor Matthew Butler explained the unique challenge of incorporating subtle VFX work into a scene where so much happens in camera. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage

“With Steven, he wants everything to be as practical as it can be,” Butler said. “We had a real train. A real train, a real car attached to that train, it was being dragged on a real track. That actually did happen.”

But while Spielberg’s preferences were clear, Butler clarified that blockbusters on this scale rarely come down to a binary choice between practical effects and VFX. The biggest scenes often contain elements of both, as the pairing between in-camera human acting and cutting edge post-production is what leads to movie magic.

“When you combine some of the live action blue screen work, clearly that’s your lead actor and actress there, and your stunt work where it’s like ‘Oh my God, that looks really real’ and the stuff that you just can’t do that’s just too dangerous … that’s where visual effects came in,” he said. “But I wouldn’t say it was a visual effects sequence. It was a sequence that contained all of those, and it came together in the right way.”

#3412. DC Officially Confirms Return Of Iconic Justice League Hero

A major Justice League icon returns with a villainous twist that may soon become a huge threat to DC's top superheroes. Several notorious DC villains have genuinely turned their lives around to earn a coveted seat inside the Justice League. For instance, Plastic Man left his origins as a small-time safecracker to become one of a Justice League mainstay, while Catwoman fought alongside the Justice League of America during the New 52 era and Killer Frost redeemed herself as a core member of Batman’s JLA squad. Most recently, the Justice League's villain amnesty plan has given foes like Lex Luthor, Starro, and Major Force a second chance.

On the other side of the spectrum, even the purest champions of the Justice League have succumbed to external corruption or moral compromises that pushed them into villainy either temporarily or permanently. Hal Jordan’s grief-fueled descent into Parallax during Emerald Twilight is still the most infamous villain turn in Justice League history to this day, alongside Maxwell Lord’s cold-blooded betrayal of the Justice League International in Countdown to Infinite Crisis and Triumph’s bitter fall after being erased from the timeline. Superman became an authoritarian tyrant in Injustice and The Justice Lords, and Mister Terrific recently ascended toward Darkseid-like godhood after absorbing the League's powers.

A Justice League heel turn is especially concerning during a moment of union for all the world's heroes, as the betraying character must have a very convincing reason to turn their back on the team.

In Deathstroke: The Terminator #9, titled "Sins of the Atom," Ray Palmer makes a dramatic entrance to confront Slade Wilson following the brutal events of the previous issue, where a disgraced Deathstroke killed a random motorist in a fit of road rage, only to discover the corpse of Green Lantern Vath Sarn locked inside the trunk. Ray Palmer has spent months secretly feeding intel to the world’s deadliest assassin out of growing bitterness over the Justice League’s recent villain-amnesty policies. But when Deathstroke refuses Ray’s order to leave the dead Lantern behind, the Atom humiliates Slade in hand-to-hand combat and flees.

Member of the Justice Society in New York City. Killed in 1994's Zero Crisis.

Active in the 853rd Century as a member of Justice Legion Alpha.

Infiltrated the Justice League as a double agent for the Crime Syndicate before being killed by Lex Luthor during Forever Evil.

DC's new focus on the Atom in morally complex storylines across multiple flagship titles is a refreshing treat for the hero. Despite possessing one of the coolest power sets in the DC Universe, Ray Palmer has often been relegated to brief supporting roles when his scientific knowledge and tools are needed, or to background crowd shots during Justice League crossovers. Now, between his disillusioned alliance with Deathstroke here and his ominous appearance perched right on Mister Terrific’s shoulder in Justice League Unlimited #27, DC is finally treating Palmer as an unpredictable major player whose brilliance and quiet frustrations could have serious consequences for the entire superhero community.

Eight decades after his comic book debut, the Atom should be one of pop culture’s most recognizable superheroes by now, especially since DC beat Marvel to the shrinking-hero concept by over two decades. Golden Age Atom Al Pratt first debuted all the way back in All-American Comics #19 in 1940, twenty-two years before Hank Pym. Silver Age physicist Ray Palmer launched in Showcase #34 in 1961, months ahead of Pym’s first Tales to Astonish appearance and over a year before Ant-Man donned his costume. Despite pioneering the subatomic superhero trope and joining the Justice League early in the Silver Age, DC's Atoms are still virtually unknown to casual audiences.

A classic Justice League hero gets a new origin story that might make them essential to the future of DC Comics' most popular timeline.

The wide popularity gap between Marvel and DC's shrinking heroes comes down almost entirely to missed big-screen opportunities rather than any flaw in the Atom as a character. While Marvel Studios turned Ant-Man into a billion-dollar theatrical trilogy and a pivotal hero in Avengers: Endgame, DC relegated Ray Palmer to supporting roles on television’s Arrow and DC’s Legends of Tomorrow and cut Ryan Choi’s subplot down to a brief cameo in Zack Snyder’s Justice League. In the comics, DC is only beginning to put Atom at the forefront, not only in titles like Justice League Unlimited, but also in Absolute Universe's Absolute Flash.

#3410. Eight Hacks Every Tidal User Should Know

I recently switched from Apple Music to Tidal, and I'm happy I made the change. The main reason is AI-made music: Tidal has stricter AI filtering than any other major streamer. The second reason is audio quality. While all major music streaming services do basically the same thing, Tidal's focus has always been on streaming music at the highest possible quality. While other streaming services have more or less "caught up" in terms of pure sonic fidelity, Tidal still is better at getting that quality to your speakers, if you know a few tricks.

If you're switching from Apple Music or Spotify to Tidal, you probably want to bring your playlists with you. Tidal points new users toward third-party transfer tools like TuneMyMusic and Soundizz. They both have a free tier, but they only transfers a few hundred songs gratis. My playlists are way bigger than that. The easy solution is to grumble and sign up for a month, then cancel when your tracks are transferred, but that didn't sit well with me. A playlist is just a collection of song names, so why should I have to pay anything to transfer it? To solve the problem, I came up with a simple script that transfers playlists from Apple Music and Spotify to Tidal. I will not be charging a fee. Here's how it works:

Download your playlist as a .txt file. You can do this directly from Apple Music under File>Library>Export Playlist. You can't from Spotify, but the free site Exportify will download any of your playlists as a spreadsheet file you can save.

Install Python on your system. Double click "install certificates" in the folder that opens after installation.

Download this script. Save it in the same file as your playlist.

Run the script: (For Mac, open Terminal. For Windows, go to the Command prompt. Type python3 on a Mac or py on Windows.) Drag the script into the terminal window and press enter. It should ask you to drag your downloaded playlist into the window next.

Sign in to Tidal. Hit "Approve" to give permission for Tidal to run the script.

Have a banana. The script is going to search for all the songs on your playlist and match them to Tidal's library, so it can take a little while. I tested it with a playlist from Apple Music with 2,397 songs. It took about 20 minutes and found 2,362 of my tracks, a 99% success rate.

Fix the leftovers: The program creates two separate text files for "orphans." One is songs it couldn't find and one is songs it might be worth double-checking manually.

If everything goes well, your large playlist should be available on Tidal.

Note: The script uses a community-created library to talk to Tidal, so it could stop working if Tidal changes things up.

Like most streaming services, Tidal has a "heart" button called "add to my collection." You can click on any track, album, or playlist to "like" and saved it. But Tidal also has a separate, somewhat mysterious "Save for Later" option that puts songs, albums, and playlists into a separate collection. There are a couple reasons for this. First, it keeps a running list of new-to-you music waiting for you on a rainy day, and secondly, it (presumably) affects your recommendation algorithm differently. While Tidal isn't open about every detail of its recommendation algorithm, I assume "save for later" has less weight (if any) on your future recommendations than "add to my collection."

On Tidal, tracks that are 100% AI-generated get an "AI" badge, earn no royalties, and are never placed on a Tidal-curated playlist. Users can flip a switch in Settings to either allow or disallow AI content, too. Simple, but there's a bit of nuance that goes beyond the on/off switch. You have to set the AI-toggle separately on each device you use Tidal on, even if it's the same account. I guess this is so I can listen to AI music in my car but not at my desk? Sadly, AI detection is not a science, so some AI-made, and partly AI-made, tracks may still get through.

If you're streaming music from a music app through Bluetooth, the output is automatically compressed to a lower quality, and your phone stays in charge, so a phone call or a notification can interrupt your music. But Tidal's Tidal Connect feature skips the middleman. Music streams directly from your wifi to your speaker and your phone becomes a remote control, so you can take a call, go for a walk, and even run out of phone battery and the music will keep playing.

Have an external device with Tidal Connect compatibility.

Make sure your speaker or other output device and phone or computer are on the same wifi network.

Click the icon again to switch back to your phone.

Plenty of wifi speakers don’t support Tidal Connect, so check before you buy. Tidal keeps the full list of supported devices on its site. There's everything there from WiiM Mini—a $99 small box that adds Tidal Connect to speakers you already own—to dCS components that cost more than a car.

Tidal Connect isn't the only way to get the highest quality audio from Tidal. You can go for an old school, wired path like I have. I play audio from my desktop and route it directly to a mixer via USB. Here's the set-up:

Settings > Streaming > Audio Quality: Max.

Sound Output: choose your mixer as the output device instead of your computer’s speakers.

Exclusive Mode: On. It’s under Sound Output > More Settings. Tidal sends audio straight to the mixer at each track’s native sample rate, without your computer resampling it or mixing in system sounds.

Force Volume. It's in the desktop app next to Exclusive Mode, under Settings > Streaming > Sound Output > More Settings. Force Volume means Tidal will always output at the highest volume. You'll be controlling the actual volume from your mixer.

To check what your mixer can handle, look at its maximum sample rate:

Mac: Open Audio MIDI Setup (in Applications > Utilities), click your mixer, and open the Format menu. The highest number listed is your ceiling.

Windows: Go to Settings > System > Sound, click your mixer, and look under Output settings > Format.

My cheap-ass mixer tops out a 16-bit/48kHz which is CD quality, but not Tidal's top of 24-bit/192kHz, but at least I can control the EQ. Speaking of...

It's much cooler to turn dials than mess with computer settings. Tidal doesn’t have an equalizer, so if you’re using Tidal Connect or a wired connection, you'll need something to shape the sound. Here are some options:

Your computer: System-wide EQ apps, like Equalizer APO on Windows or SoundSource on Mac, can adjust Tidal’s output. They don’t work with Tidal Connect though, which bypasses your computer’s audio processing.

Your speaker’s app: If you use a Tidal Connect speaker or streamer, it probably has a companion app for EQ.

A mixer or audio interface: Channel EQ knobs let you adjust bass, mids, and treble by hand, in real time.

Your speakers: Many powered speakers and studio monitors have low and high controls on the back.

A stereo receiver or amp: Old-school bass and treble knobs still work in 2026.

Most of Tidal's catalog streams as "better-than-CD quality" FLAC files at every subscription tier, so you might be inclined to click "play music at highest quality on everything." but settings are only as good as the gear you're using, and there are times when lower quality is the right choice. Here's when to turn down the settings:

When you're in your car: CarPlay and Bluetooth cut audio down to CD quality or less before it reaches your speaker, and with road noises, it usually doesn't matter anyway, so turn the streaming down to "High" instead of "Max." Or download your playlist before you leave, if you must have "as good as possible" audio.

You have a data cap and are off wifi. Top quality audio requires huge file transfer, so set your mobile data to High or Low and save Max for wifi.

Your connection is spotty: To avoid buffering, a lower setting keeps the music playing.

This isn't a universal hack, but some Android phones have microSD card slots, which can save you a lot of hassle if you're downloading a lot of audio files—an album at high quality might top 1GB, so having an external source will save you a ton of hassle. If your phone has a microSD card slot, go to Tidal's settings, find "download destination" and choose the memory card.

#3409. Star Wars Is Getting an Official IMAX 70mm Release for the First Time

For Star Wars 50th anniversary, Lucasfilm is going big

Han will shoot first in 70 mm IMAX when the original Star Wars returns to movie theaters next year. Lucasfilm and IMAX have confirmed that the 50th anniversary rerelease of Star Wars will be on the biggest screens possible next February, giving fans a strong reason to return to theaters.

In an official announcement on StarWars.com, Lucasfilm says Star Wars "will be shown across a select number of IMAX 70 mm film locations as well as playing in select theaters for a limited time."

That's not the only Star Wars release getting the deluxe IMAX treatment next year. Lucasfilm and IMAX reconfirmed that next year's stand-alone adventure Star Wars: Starfighter is also coming to the large-screen format. On May 28, 2027, Lucasfilm will release Star Wars: Starfighter, which was filmed for IMAX, shot with IMAX-certified film cameras, and converted to IMAX 70 mm film prints for release in a select number of IMAX film locations, according to an official announcement.

Star Wars: Starfighter is directed by Shawn Levy (Deadpool & Wolverine, Stranger Things) and stars Ryan Gosling (Blade Runner 2049, Barbie) as Kade Auberon, "a cynical rogue" who is "hurled into a dangerous adventure across the galaxy that puts him on a crash course with destiny." Starfighter also stars Matt Smith, Mia Goth, Aaron Pierre, Jamael Westman, Daniel Ings, Flynn Gray, and Amy Adams. The movie was written by Jonathan Tropper (Warrior, The Adam Project).

IMAX previously confirmed a 2027 release for the original Star Wars. It will be a rare opportunity to see George Lucas' 1977 science-fantasy epic that changed cinema without the alterations and digital effects that were added years after the fact.

Lucas has become infamous for going back and tinkering with the edits and special effects throughout the original Star Wars trilogy. For the 20th anniversary of the franchise, Lucasfilm primed the pump for the release of Star Wars: The Phantom Menace with a monthly theatrical re-release of the Star Wars “Special Edition” trilogy, which saw robust changes and even additional scenes rendered with then-state-of-the-art computer graphics. Lucas continued to futz with Star Wars for the next three decades, which is how we wound up with the “Maclunkey Cut” of A New Hope on Disney Plus.

In 2025, former Lucasfilm boss Kathleen Kennedy teamed up with the British Film Institute to screen a print of Star Wars said to be the earliest cut of the original that existed, untouched by its creator’s impulses to "perfect" it. The BFI even went an extra step in preparing the film reels for projection, finding an old, complete version of the original crawl, before "A New Hope" was added to the title, to run in front of the film.

After Lucasfilm teased plans to bring Star Wars back to theaters, longtime fans wondered which version of the film they'd get. Lucas himself had said that the original versions "will disappear" and, in his mind, the unaltered versions "[don't] really exist anymore." Fans who bemoan Lucas' additions and alterations to Star Wars have been resigned to relying on old VHS and Laserdisc copies, or pieced-together versions restored by fans, for decades now.

But soon, they'll have a chance to see the original on a brand-new scale — if they can get tickets.

Star Wars returns to movie theaters on Feb. 19, 2027.

#3408. Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage

Looks like Hollywood could be heading into the new year with relief on a national level. The push to pass a federal film and television tax credit by the end of 2026 picked up momentum on Friday at a White House press conference, where President Trump said his administration was actively negotiating the measure and predicted it would pass.

“It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump said. He singled out Senator Adam Schiff, the California Democrat who introduced the bill with Republican Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina back in September, and said, “I tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’ Adam Schiff said that.” Related Stories Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Debuts to Mighty $120 Million, Reviving Lionsgate’s Most Important Franchise Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Crosses $100 Million Globally

Trump mentioned Georgia and New Jersey by name as states with good tax credits for film and TV production, but argued that those incentives alone would not bring enough production work back from overseas. With a federal credit, he said, “Hollywood would open again.”

Trump said his administration was also negotiating whether to extend the measure to benefit movie theaters, but said the matter was unsettled. He first publicly called for a federal production incentive in August after meeting with actor Jon Voight: one of three industry “special ambassadors” he appointed early last year.

The bill’s sponsors announced more than 60 new House cosponsors and four new Senate cosponsors on Thursday morning — with lawmakers from both parties signing on in both chambers. The following day, Trump himself brought up the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act in response to a question about whether he could work with Democrats. Calling the bill “very bipartisan,” he said, “I can tell you right now it’s going to happen.”

Trump gave no timetable, though earlier this week, Representative Linda Sánchez, one of the bill’s House sponsors from California, called for Congress to pass it before 2027 so productions could qualify for benefits on the first of the year.

“Members of both parties have watched jobs in their districts move overseas,” she said in a release from Schiff’s office sent to the press. “Momentum is on our side, and we need to strike while the iron is hot by passing this bill before the end of the year.”

A floor vote has yet to be announced, but multiple sources told IndieWire the measure would move faster if attached to a stopgap government funding bill. If passed and approved, the federal initiative would give qualifying film and TV productions a 20 percent credit on labor expenses for American workers. The credit could reach 30 percent for productions that qualify for bonuses.

For crews accustomed to watching projects follow tax breaks to Canada or the U.K., the proposal would give producers a clear financial incentive to keep that work here for them in the U.S. The bill’s new Senate cosponsors include Republicans Katie Britt of Alabama and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — as well as Democrats Chris Coons of Delaware and Dick Durbin of Illinois.

The AFL-CIO and the American Hotel & Lodging Association also endorsed the bill, joining a coalition that already included IATSE, SAG-AFTRA, the Directors Guild of America, and the Motion Picture Association.

“Given the support from Republicans and Democrats in both chambers and the president, we can get this legislation across the finish line,” Schiff said.

#3406. Stephen King’s R-Rated Sci-Fi Series Is Officially Darker Than His Book

Most Stephen King novels dabble with incredibly grim subject matter. Owing to this, it is an impressive feat when an adaptation manages to push the boundaries of darkness even further. Quite a few movie and TV adaptations of the author's work have managed to defy expectations and deliver even bleaker stories. Case in point, 2007's The Mist leaves viewers with a completely hopeless ending.

While MGM+'s The Institute does not match the extremes of Frank Darabont's The Mist, it does push the darker elements of the original story to a new level. In season 1, The Institute felt more like a watered-down version of the original. It stayed true to the original themes and character beats of the book but featured less graphic violence and psychological horror.

From a visual standpoint, even The Institute season 2 is not too different. Despite its TV-MA rating, the show rarely pushes its disturbing imagery to match Stephen King's writing. In terms of storytelling, however, the show has officially exceeded the darker aspects of the book, which makes it even more compelling than it initially seemed.

In Stephen King's The Institute, the main young characters overcome the overarching evil forces towards the end. They take down the very facility that tortured them and emerge victorious in their battle for freedom. The Institute season 1's ending portrays something similar, where Luke and his friends destroy the titular facility, albeit with a few big losses.

However, in season 2, their victory is completely stripped. They soon realize that they are dealing with far bigger forces. The facility they destroyed was a mere pawn in a far bigger conspiracy. After jumping out of the proverbial frying pan in season 1, they realize they are now on the fire with powerful people deadset upon finding them.

The main character, Luke, also came off as a steadfast hero. He always took a stand against the people running the Institute and did not hold himself back from going all-out against them. In season 2, he is cursed with the power of foresight. His precognition abilities improve, allowing him to see how his decisions could even get his friends killed.

As a result, instead of throwing all caution to the wind, he makes some moral compromises and plays safe. He even betrays his friends, believing that it would help him save them from their imminent doom. Speaking of doom, The Institute season 2 also does not shy away from killing off one of season 1's main heroes, Wendy, in the very beginning.

These developments instantly establish the high and incredibly bleak stakes The Institute's main characters are now dealin with.

Expanding the original story of a complete book can always be a tricky endeavor. Even some of the greatest adaptations, like Game of Thrones, have suffered after extending beyond their source material. Fortunately, for The Institute, it followed a fairly generic and derivative storyline in season 1 while introducing some intriguing ideas.

This paved the way for the series to become all the more compelling in season 2. So far, The Institute has been doing an incredible job of expanding ideas surrounding precognition, free will, and determinism in season 2. This allows the series to be even more thought-provoking than the original Stephen King book. It almost feels like a Philip K. Dick adaptation in its ongoing story beats.

Hopefully, moving forward, The Institute season 2 will only get better. Instead of treading the same path as its predecessor and relying on familiar ideas from the sci-fi genre, the Stephen King adaptation should take more creative risks and not shy away from being as dark (if not more) as the original book.

The Institute, released in 2025, follows 14-year-old genius Luke Ellis, who is kidnapped and wakes up at a mysterious facility filled with children possessing unusual abilities. Meanwhile, Tim Jamieson, a former police officer, seeks a fresh start in a nearby town, inevitably intertwining his fate with Luke's.

#3405. Eight Important Router Settings You Should Check (or Change)

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Your router is a key piece of your home network, as it connects all of your other devices to the internet. This also makes it a highly valuable target for attackers and can leave your data vulnerable—especially if you simply plug your router in with its default settings unchanged. Whether your router is brand new or it's been a while since you audited your existing setup, these are the key settings to check and change right now.

Your router's security protocol determines how encryption and authentication work to protect data that's transmitted over your network. WPA3 Personal is the newest standard and the most secure, so if it's available on your router, enable it. It's compatible with devices that support Wi-Fi 6. Some older devices may not work with WPA3, in which case the WPA2/WPA3 Transitional mixed mode is a good alternative. At minimum, set your router to WPA2 Personal (AES).

Some routers ship with factory default login credentials, which are the username and password you need to access your device's admin dashboard. (This is not the same as your network name or wifi password, which you set up later.) Default router passwords are searchable online, which leaves your router's admin settings open to anyone. Once you get into your dashboard for the first time, change the default credentials and enable two-factor authentication for your admin account if available.

While some newer routers do have unique, device-specific defaults, it's a good idea to check this setting and ensure it's secure. If you're prompted to create custom admin credentials during the setup process, do it.

Your network name, or SSID, is how your network appears when you search for available wifi. By default, this may be the name of the router brand or a short string of characters, but you should choose something unique to your network. Make sure there's no identifying personal information, such as your name or house number. While you may be tempted to hide your network and obscure your SSID, this may actually make your information less secure, so keep this setting disabled. You can, however, add "_nomap" to the end of your network name, which prevents your router's physical coordinates from being mapped by location databases.

The password to access your network should also be unique and secure and should not include obvious personal information. One option to keep it memorable and easy to type is to create a passphrase using five to seven unrelated words that, combined, have at least 16 characters.

Being able to log into your router's admin dashboard from anywhere may be useful if you have complex networking needs or troubleshooting issues that often have to be addressed when you're away from home, but it also leaves an entry point open for attackers. Turn off remote management to prevent anyone from accessing your dashboard unless they are on your network. (This is also a great reason to have strong, unique admin credentials.)

Two additional settings that leave your network vulnerable are Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) and Universal Plug and Play (UPnP). The former lets users connect to your network with a PIN, which can be vulnerable to brute-force attacks. The latter allows smart devices to easily connect to your network—but this also allows malware to spread more readily. You may need to have UPnP on in order to connect devices initially but should disable it afterward.

Any easy win for your network security is segmenting traffic to different networks, so if one is compromised, the data on the others remain unaffected. Many wifi routers have a "guest mode," which creates a separate SSID and password that you can share with visitors instead of giving them your primary network credentials. You can also set up a separate network for all of your smart home and IoT devices so exploitable vulnerabilities in these devices don't put your computers, phones, and other connected devices at risk too.

Routers run a type of software—called firmware—just like any other device. Firmware controls the router's core functions and is not immune to vulnerabilities, which can be exploited by bad actors. And, just like other types of software, manufacturers occasionally push updates to patch these flaws. Check your router's dashboard to see if automatic updates are toggled on. Some devices require an opt-in for auto updates during setup, so you should enable them if they are off. Some routers may even require manual updates—in this case, set a monthly or quarterly (at minimum) calendar reminder to check for patches.

#3404. 34 Years Later, the Best 'Far Side' Quote Will Still Leave You Speechless

Brian VanHooker is a Pop Culture Writer specializing in Celebrity Interviews and In-Depth Oral Histories in the areas of Comedy, TV, Film, Cartoons, Comic Books, 80s/90s Nostalgia, Fatherhood, Retro Games and Food (especially Pizza). He was the Senior Features Writer at Cracked and a Staff Writer at MEL. He has written for Inverse, Inside Hook, Maxim, Men's Health, Fatherly, SFGate and more. He's the co-creator of the comic book/cartoon Barnum & Elwood and The Tramp, an award-winning comedy pilot starring John O’Hurley. He also hosts a TMNT interview podcast called Turtle Tracks and was once called a “Good Guy” by Mr. T.

In recent months, I’ve been examining the best-ever quotes from various newspaper comic strips, and in that time I’ve determined that every comic strip requires its own approach. For Charles Schulz’s Peanuts, I chose something heartfelt and inspirational because those comics and characters really have inspired people. For Bill Watterson’s Calvin and Hobbes, I investigated something more philosophical, as the best of those comics make the audience contemplate human nature and the world around them. But for Gary Larson’s The Far Side, the task is monumentally different.

Larson didn’t do deep and inspirational. Many of his cartoons required you to think, but not because they were thoughtful. Larson’s work was brilliant, and it sometimes took a few minutes to figure out what the punchline was. Take, this comic strip where an artist is painting a woman as a half-fly creature, for example. You likely see the woman or the painting first, and you wonder why the artist is painting her that way. Only after inspecting the comic more closely do you see the dead fly stuck to his glasses.

Larson’s work often requires the reader to investigate something, but usually not in any kind of overly deep way.

The Far Side is brilliant, but it's not the kind of comic strip that makes you ponder life’s big questions. Larson channeled his genius into joke-telling, and that’s what made The Far Side so sharply funny. As such, determining Larson’s best-ever Far Side quote shouldn’t be some insightful, inspirational, or thoughtful journey — even though I did try going that way at first.

I thought maybe the quote should come from a comic about God, as several Far Side comics feature God as a character. But after reading a bunch of Larson’s God comics, I determined that God actually isn’t all that deep or interesting. Sometimes he’s just kind of a jerk.

Then I thought to look up comics about death, thinking that maybe Larson had something profound to say on the subject. Given Larson’s signature macabre style of humor, death is featured frequently in The Far Side, but nothing seemed all that weighty or important. I finally abandoned this approach when I found a comic where a snake hanged himself with his own body.

That’s when I gave up on going deep and decided to just find something funny. But there are thousands of Far Side comics, and Larson’s humor varied. Sometimes he was dark, sometimes he was silly, sometimes he deconstructed a well-known saying or song or other pop culture reference. So I tried to find a quote that did all — or at least most of — what Larson was known for. Also, I wanted a quote where the visual wasn’t required to get the joke. Larson’s work was highly visual, and with generally just one panel, it often had the visual as the setup and the caption as the punchline. If I was looking for the best ever Far Side comic, it would be one where the visual and the caption work in concert. But while trying to find the best-ever quote, I wanted something where the image was not required.

For a little while I thought about going with “Welcome to hell… here’s your accordion,” from a comic which shows Heaven and Hell. In Heaven, you’re given a harp, but in Hell you’re given an accordion. I liked this because it’s very dark and silly, and it’s the kind of thing you’d only find in The Far Side. Eventually though I softened on it because the visual is still the stronger element in this one. The line comes off as basically a funny non-sequitur without the visual. To get the whole joke about how accordions are terrible instruments, you really need the contrast.

After abandoning that comic, I found this one from 1992 and realized it was the perfect fit. The image shows a mime under a falling tree and the caption reads:

“Question: If a tree falls in the forest and no one’s around, and it hits a mime, does anyone care?”

I think this is the one because it’s funny, because it's dark, because it's silly, and because it takes a well-known idiom — the tree falling in the woods question — and turns it into a punchline. That may not do everything that Larson did, but it’s a lot of his very best qualities all in one place.

And, unlike the vast majority of Far Side comics, it’s more about the words than the image. Larson’s gags were almost always visual, or at least relied on a visual component to get his jokes across. For this comic, I’d argue that you don’t need the visual at all. Sure, the drawing is funny, but in no way is it required. Also, this quote is entirely lacking in emotional or philosophical depth, which is precisely what you want when you’re reading The Far Side.

#3403. If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It

The uproar over the alleged use of generative AI imagery in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” has taken a familiar path. Early responses to the Netflix film penned by Quentin Tarantino and directed by David Fincher have pointed out egregious examples of generative video artifacts sticking out in key flashback moments in the film — including one shot from the trailer where it certainly looks like a video AI program rendered a wagon the wrong way around.

The criticism is of the use of generative AI in principle as a fundamental betrayal of the creative process — but it’s also of Fincher, as a director who, historically, has been meticulous with the level of detail and intention in every single shot of his films. In the early responses to Fincher’s latest, there’s been a lot of surprise and disappointment about this particular filmmaker being caught up in an AI controversy. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Debuts to Mighty $120 Million, Reviving Lionsgate’s Most Important Franchise Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Crosses $100 Million Globally

At first blush, his approach seems at odds with using generative AI video, which relies on regurgitated (and, it bears repeating every time, stolen) data. But Fincher has defended his use of AI to the LA Times as a way to continue to innovate on an art form that is, after all, just over a hundred years old.

That defense really shouldn’t be surprising, given Fincher’s history with AI specifically. Although he’s been critical of generative tools in the past, Fincher admitted to using them (never publicly disclosing which) in the 4K remaster of “Se7en,” which the director described as a process of needing to remake the negative in order to battle the ravages of time (and the thousands of tiny scratches that would show up in 4K). “If you could see a 30-year-old negative and what it looks like even when immaculately stored — it was an enormous amount of fixing, just digs and scratches and cinch,” he told EW at the time.

That kind of image restoration technology was around long, long before the Anthropic IPO failed to save the stock market, but its level of precision has increased enormously in the past year. There were also sequences in the stored “Se7en,” though, where generative tech filled in gaps from the original. For one example, Fincher talked about a moment where a camera pan overshot the mark and changedh a shot. The performance had been good enough to use a technically flawed take — and, combined wit an unused take, allowed software to generate the missing information and restore the intended image.

“It ends up being the most thrillingly stupid fix in the world because if you see it, we didn’t do our jobs. And you probably won’t see it. You probably won’t be aware that it’s happened. But you look at it, and you just think to yourself, ‘It’s so nice that we can fix that kind of stuff today,'” Fincher told Collider about that moment in “Se7en.”

By Fincher’s own lights, then, the problem with AI in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is that people are painfully aware of it. AI critics might make a distinction between video restoration tools that work on existing projects and those tools being used because they can more quickly and cheaply generate originals that would’ve otherwise needed to be crafted by human hands. Having something AI-generated isn’t necessarily better than nothing when it comes to art, and choosing to AI-generate a Western chase sequence inside of, say, 10 seconds isn’t a solution to all.

Still, Fincher knows what he’s doing. This past week, he emphasized to the LA Times that he’s not a Luddite when it comes to film: “We’re talking about a thing that’s a hundred years old, and everyone’s going, ‘Stop. Pencils down. No more iterating. It’s not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person’s eyes.’ Well, it exists. Should we not use it?”

The answer is an emphatic “No!” to some And they can certainly be mad, or disappointed, or disheartened about Fincher’s decision to use AI tools. The one thing they shouldn’t be is surprised.

#3401. The iPhone Duo Is Getting Face Unlock

Apple dropped iOS 27.2.1 last week, patching a handful of security vulnerabilities and bugs—including two iMessage flaws that let people read messages they shouldn't. But while most of us are running this version (or should install it as soon as possible), others are running something different—iOS 27.3.

Apple is currently beta testing the third major update in the iOS 27 era, and anyone—developer and public tester alike—is free to install it at their leisure. With it, comes the return of the Health app, vertical Safari tabs, and Siri AI app actions, among other new features. But for users of Apple's first foldable, the iPhone Duo, iOS 27.3 brings two rather notable changes—both of which are for the better.

With the second iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple is introducing face unlock for the iPhone Duo. The foldable famously ships with Touch ID, the first new iPhone since the third-gen iPhone SE to do so. While that isn't a problem per se, many of us are used to unlocking our iPhones with our faces. This update just lets new Duo owners keep up with that muscle memory.

Now, take note: This isn't Face ID. No software update can introduce new hardware, so the iPhone Duo still doesn't have the camera tech required to power Apple's Face ID system. As such, the Duo's face unlock is likely not as secure as Face ID on other iPhones. Perhaps that's why your iPhone Duo will require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. This feature seems to be one of pure convenience: If you want to be able to unlock your Duo with your face (at least, some of the time), you can.

What's more, this isn't a default setting. If you're running the beta, or if you're reading this after iOS 27.3 drops, you can find the option in Settings > Touch ID & Passcode.

Apple made a big deal about the continuity involved with opening and closing the iPhone Duo. As you do, your content moves with you seamlessly—a very Apple thing to do. That said, you might expect folding the Duo to lock it, but it doesn't. You need to hit the side button to actually put the phone to sleep.

iOS 27.3 changes that. If you so choose, you can enable a setting to lock your Duo whenever you close it. That won't work for everyone, of course—some users may still want to move between modes without worrying about locking their Duos. But for those who would rather lock their devices whenever they fold them up, the new option is under Settings > Display & Brightness.

#3400. All 62 Episodes Of Prime Video's Sci-Fi Masterpiece Are Perfect From Start To Finish

All 62 episodes of Prime Video's acclaimed sci-fi masterpiece deliver gripping interplanetary warfare, extraordinary characters, and epic storytelling. Released back in 2015, this dystopian sci-fi series spanned six seasons on Prime Video until it concluded in 2022, based on a series of celebrated novels that began with 2011's Leviathan Wakes. Praised for its elite world-building, science-backed mechanisms, and great visuals, this is one sci-fi series that all fans of the genre must check out, as all 62 episodes are truly perfect from start to finish.

The Expanse is a true sci-fi masterpiece on Prime Video, given its 95% Rotten Tomatoes score across 62 episodes and 6 seasons. The series delivers peak dystopian sci-fi on streaming and still sets the gold standard for the genre 11 years after its premiere on Prime Video. Critics and audiences agree that it is, somewhat quietly, one of the greatest sci-fi series of the 21st century, with The Ringer saying of its final season, "For all the worthy comparisons to Game of Thrones, there's one thing The Expanse achieved that its HBO counterpart couldn't: This show stuck the landing." For a complete sci-fi binge that's worth the investment, The Expanse can't be beat.

The Expanse has one of the most intriguing premises with a massive scope in all modern sci-fi set between conflicting communities on Earth and in outer space. With each competing for political power and cosmic influence, The Expanse is set several centuries in the future, when humans have colonized several areas of the solar system, including Mars and the Asteroid Belt between Mars and Jupiter.

When the series begins, Earth remains the most dominant force within the solar system, but a newly advanced society and military presence on Mars threatens to disrupt that order. Earth's key vulnerability, however, is its dependence on off-planet resources from far-off colonies.

Much like the distribution of power between nations on Earth, colonies each import, export, and trade resources, which become the driving forces behind power and control in this new dynamic. This is one of the ways that The Expanse feels reality-based and plausible given the circumstances, while also maintaining modern science elements that never lean too heavily into the fantasy genre.

Even the battles that take place in outer space are based on realistic physics, separating it from other epic space franchises such as Dune and Star Wars. This emphasis on political considerations and resource allocation resembles the most crucial and basic foundation of human civilization and conflicts between world superpowers.

While The Expanse carries a vast scale across planets and colonies, the heart of the series throughout all six seasons is the crew of the Rocinante spaceship. Featuring members from Earth, Mars, and the Belt, the crew forms an unlikely bond and allegiance despite their cultural differences, which forms the emotional core of the series. Several key figures include James Holden (Steven Strait), an ex-military officer and captain of the ship, Naomi Nagata (Dominique Tipper), an engineer from the Belt, Amos Burton (Wes Chatham), a mechanic from Earth, and Alex Kamal (Cas Anvar), a pilot from Mars.

All 26 episodes of Netflix's sci-fi masterpiece series deliver a mind-bending mystery, extraordinary storytelling, and a deeply satisfying conclusion.

These four begin on the Canterbury, a freighter ship transporting water from Saturn's rings to the Belt, which is destroyed in season 1. James, Naomi, Amos, and Alex must work together to survive and discover who destroyed the Canterbury and why. As their journey continues, they eventually come into possession of a Martian gunship they rename the Rocinante, a reference to the famous 1605 novel Don Quixote. All this only scratches the surface of the characters and story in The Expanse, which has a new prequel series set to be released in 2027.
