#3399. Robert Pattinson's Forgotten Dark Fantasy Thriller Proves He's a Perfect James Bond

Not everybody is convinced Robert Pattinson is the right choice to be the next James Bond. Some are complaining Bond should be played by someone less famous, like he has in the past. Others feel he’s not masculine enough, or good-looking enough, or charismatic enough. Most of all, though, it seems many people don't love the idea that “the Twilight guy” is playing Bond.

Honestly, I do think there is some merit to the idea that Bond should be played by an up-and-comer, if only because that’s been the tradition. (Clearly Amazon, which took over the franchise in 2025, has other ideas.) As for the more cosmetic complaints, I guess those all come down to personal taste.

As for the Twilight-related concerns, I understand them because, when Pattinson was announced as Batman back in 2019, I thought​​​​​​​ “Oh no, the Twilight guy? How could this guy, who seemed so…soft, be the Dark Knight?” I hated the idea. Then, a few months after the announcement, I saw the Robert Eggers film The Lighthouse and completely changed my mind.

The Lighthouse, which is currently streaming on HBO Max, is generally described as a horror film or as psychological horror with some fantasy elements, but I found it to be more of a comedy than anything else. I honestly think that, up until The Lighthouse, I’d literally never seen Pattinson in a movie before. Literally nothing I’d heard of with him had appealed to me, so it wasn’t Pattinson that lured me to The Lighthouse. Part of the reason I went to see The Lighthouse was Willem Dafoe, who I love. Another factor was a review I’d read by film critic Tim Grierson, who described​​​​​​​ the movie as “a terrific comedy about having a terrible roommate.” As a fan of The Odd Couple who regularly laments a lack of comedies in theaters, that was enough to convince me to check it out.

The Lighthouse really is just about two guys in a lighthouse dealing with the loneliness of the job, which requires them to be stuck at sea for weeks at a time. Dafoe plays a grouchy old sea-dog, while Pattinson is his young apprentice. The movie is a laugh riot, with lots of drinking, some wild singing, and both men becoming increasingly unhinged. One dreams he has sex with a mermaid, the other masturbates all the time, and both are brought to their breaking point by the end.

To be clear, nothing about Pattinson’s character in The Lighthouse made me think that he would be the perfect Batman. His character is a young man who’s green to this profession, but he’s a bit jaded from past failures and secretive about his personal life. He's fairly serious at the beginning, but he jumps into a rage more and more as the film progresses. I guess there’s some overlap with Bruce Wayne/Batman there, but not very much.

The reason why The Lighthouse convinced me of Pattinson's ability to be Batman was that he completely disappears into the role. Mere minutes into the movie, I entirely forgot who I was watching and any skepticism I ever had about the guy. Of course, the mustache and 19th-century New England accent helped with that, but it was more than that. Robert Pattinson is just one of those actors who can completely disappear into a role without any trace of the guy you thought you knew. As much as that’s the desire for any acting role, it doesn’t really happen quite that often, but Pattinson does it in The Lighthouse and I’ve seen him do it in several films since.

Of course, with Pattinson in the news right now, a lot of his movies are being recommended, and while I love him in The Batman, The Odyssey, Tenet, and others, all of those movies have a lot of plot and action going on. In contrast, The Lighthouse​​​​​​​ is pretty bare-bones. You get to see two guys just acting without much else to distract from it.

The chemistry between Pattinson and Dafoe is also just fantastic. Those two are so funny and interesting together, especially when they are at each other’s throats. It kind of makes me hope for a Lighthouse reunion in one of Pattinson's​​​​​​​ Bond films, with Dafoe cast as a Bond villain. I mean, Dafoe feels like a guy who would make a perfect Bond villain anyway, and, given his chemistry with Pattinson, I think that would be really exciting to see.​​​​​​​

Perhaps I’m getting ahead of myself a little bit there, but if you, like I did, think of Pattinson as nothing more than that Twilight guy, I’m telling you, you’re wrong, and you only need to see him have sex with a mermaid to wipe that impression clean from your mind​​​​​​​.

The Lighthouse is available to stream on HBO Max

#3398. Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Crosses $100 Million Globally

“You Can See Everything,” an unconventional documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in exile, has crossed $100 million at the global box office. Its success extends a hot streak for A24, the indie studio behind last summer’s blockbuster “Backrooms” as well as arthouse hits such as “The Drama” and “Primetime.”

“You Can See Everything” now ranks as the eighth-highest grossing non-music documentary, moving ahead of “Deep Sea 3D,” and the second-highest grossing non-music and non-nature documentary, behind Michael Moore’s “Fahrenheit 9/11.” It’s unlikely to surpass Moore’s anti-Bush jeremiad, which grossed an astonishing $222.4 million when it opened in the height of a fiercely contested presidential election. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage

Those aren’t the only benchmarks with which to measure “You Can See Everything’s” impact. It is now the seventh-highest grossing film in the history of A24, coming in behind “Materialists,” which earned $105.6 million globally. On a domestic basis, “You Can See Everything” is A24’s third-highest grossing film, ranking just behind “Backrooms” ($197.5 million) and “Marty Supreme” ($96 million). It should easily surpass “Marty Supreme” and that film had Timothée Chalamet and a boatload of Oscar noms behind it.

“You Can See Everything,” which is co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, earned $2.5 million this weekend to bring its domestic haul to $93.5 million after six weeks of release. Most of its earnings have been stateside. It’s currently playing in Australia, the U.K., and Scandinavia and the studio said its international rollout will continue over the next several weeks.

A24 is trying to keep the hits coming with “Club Kid.” Jordan Firstman’s look at a party promoter forced to grow up when he discovers he has a son, grossed $1.4 million on 229 screens in limited release this weekend. It has earned $3.4 million since it debuted three weeks ago. A24 bought the film out of Cannes for $17 million.

#3395. Crunchyroll Has A New #1 Anime, And It Blows One Piece Out Of The Water

One Piece has grown accustomed to being at the top of charts, but Crunchyroll has unveiled a major competitor. Frieren: Beyond Journey's End is the most popular series on the streaming service, according to Crunchyroll's list of most popular anime. One Piece is trailing behind at number six, as of the time of writing.

While it's nothing unusual for anime to temporarily displace one of the greats of the Big Three, Frieren's dominance has been well above par. Since the premiere of Frieren: Beyond Journey's End's anime back in 2023, the series has been constantly at the forefront of best-of lists and has regularly been the most popular anime on services like Netflix—in fact, the anime has retained a steady 100% on Rotten Tomatoes since its launch.

This also isn't the first time that Frieren has dethroned One Piece, with Frieren and Jujutsu Kaisen outpacing One Piece's manga sales in 2026 per ORICON's midterm 2026 report. All of these data points indicate something much larger than Frieren's individual quality; it represents Frieren's unique role within a broader cultural zeitgeist, and dethroning One Piece on Crunchyroll might just be the latest development that can prove that point.

On the surface, Frieren: Beyond Journey's End and One Piece might not seem to share much in common. One Piece's story hardly needs rehashing; the long-running shōnen juggernaut is an action-adventure series based on the scruffy pirate Luffy and the Straw Hat Crew as they travel the world in search of a mythical ultimate treasure called the One Piece so that Luffy can become King of the Pirates.

Frieren, on the other hand, chronicles the adventures of the elven mage Frieren, who sets off on a journey to collect spells after her party had once defeated the Demon King. The catch is that elves age particularly slowly in Frieren, living over 1000 years; her initial 50-year journey felt like a blip for her until she reunites with her party and sees them in old age. After the death of the party's hero Himmel, Frieren sets out on another journey and slowly assembles a new gang of friends, this time aiming to understand human emotions, experience, and mortality.

Frieren: Beyond Journey's End has become one of the biggest titles in anime in recent years, and her English voice actress knows just why it blew up.

There isn't obvious connective tissue between the two series; to find it, one has to dig a bit deeper. One Piece's world-building is second to none, and it's inarguable that the shōnen massively raised the bar for what stories popular series could tell. One Piece didn't develop in a vacuum—its storytelling and worldbuilding are a continuation of predecessors like Hunter x Hunter and Dragon Ball.

Frieren didn't develop in a vacuum, either; its emotional resonances and character depth reflect conventions that One Piece played a massive role in making viable cornerstones of shōnen storytelling.

Perhaps there's no better example than One Piece's iconic Fan Letter special, in which the lives, environments, and consequences of the events taking place in One Piece's main story are intimately explored. That level of depth, retrospection, and introspection is precisely the motor powering Frieren under the hood, and it's the reason the series has become so successful. It's not so much that Frieren outshines One Piece; it's more that Frieren lovingly builds on the foundation One Piece has spent years laying.

There's also something to be said about how a series like Frieren can ring true with some of One Piece's most satisfying emotional contrasts. Like One Piece, Frieren can be light and digestible, but it can also feel epic, dark, and all too human. Frieren sets those emotional contrasts to work in a vastly different context—one where they're arguably far more focused and intentional.

In a fun turn of events, series like Frieren can therefore turn into thematic gateways for casual anime fans to try a series like One Piece, whose sheer length might otherwise intimidate them. One Piece, for all intents and purposes, has a long-standing and steadily growing fanbase. Taking into account how the anime industry has boomed since the pandemic largely thanks to streaming libraries, it makes sense why tight, bingeable seasonal releases like Frieren might briefly overtake long-running episodic series like One Piece, which now numbers nearly 1200 episodes.

However, Frieren's continued (and repeated) success can't be chalked up to a simple fluke. It's legitimately an absolute anime masterpiece that takes some of One Piece's most beloved features, dials them in, and flawlessly executes a deeply human journey all its own. Taking over giants like One Piece on Crunchyroll is a massive milestone to be celebrated, and for Frieren: Beyond Journey's End, it's well-deserved.

#3392. Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Debuts to Mighty $120 Million, Reviving Lionsgate’s Most Important Franchise

“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” made quick work of the competition, debuting to an impressive $120 million and easily capturing the top spot on the domestic box office chart.

The sequel represents a massive improvement on the opening of its predecessor, 2023’s “The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes,” which bowed with $44 million, a franchise low. However, “Sunrise on the Reaping” didn’t match the highs of the series. Its opening pales in comparison to 2013’s “Catching Fire” ($158 million debut), 2012’s OG “Hunger Games” ($152.5 million), and 2014’s “Mockingjay Part 1” ($121.8 million debut). Deadline trumpeted the fact that the film has the second highest-grossing opening for a prequel behind “Rogue One,” which seems like a milestone no one really ever thought or cared about before. So extra credit to some enterprising studio publicist or Google for unearthing that gem. Related Stories Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Crosses $100 Million Globally If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It

But whatever records it holds, “Sunrise on the Reaping” has revived a series that was looking a little long in the tooth. Why did this “Hunger Games” outpace “The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes”? It probably helped that franchise icons Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, and Woody Harrelson were coaxed back for brief appearances. There was also a top-shelf cast that included Oscar winner Kieran Culkin, Oscar nominees Glenn Close, Elle Fanning, Ralph Fiennes, and Jesse Plemons, and rising stars like Iris Apatow, Mckenna Grace, Ben Wang, and Joseph Zada. Internationally, “Sunrise on the Reaping” earned $105 million from 84 territories, pushing its worldwide box office gross to $225 million.

Lionsgate is distributing the $150 million production, as it has the previous films. The studio recently mounted something of a comeback under Adam Fogelson, who replaced Joe Drake as the motion picture chief in 2024. Lionsgate was on its back foot at the time, having released flops like “Borderlands” and the reboot of “The Crow.” In recent months, its fortunes have shifted thanks to blockbusters like “Michael” and hits such as “The Housemaid” and “The Long Walk.” A revived “Hunger Games” franchise is critical, as it gives Lionsgate another pillar for its slate.

But “The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes” success threatened to overshadow “I Play Rocky.” The Amazon MGM Studios release earned $9.3 million after expanding from 29 locations to 2,477 theaters. It’s playing like gangbusters, earning an A+ CinemaScore, a rare distinction that puts it in the company of “Top Gun: Maverick” and “The Avengers.” The word-of-mouth is clearly excellent, which could help it build momentum over the holidays. It’s also worth noting that “I Play Rocky” is catering to older moviegoers who take their time getting around to seeing things. Even if it starts to fade, “I Play Rocky” is a relatively economical bet. It cost in the $30 million range to produce and has earned $10.4 million since it debuted.

Then there’s “Ebenezer.” The Johnny Depp revival isn’t as glorious as his most diehard fans may have hoped. The Christmas story fell roughly 60 percent in its second weekend, earning $7.7 million to bring its domestic total to $32.5 million. But Paramount didn’t spend lavishly to make the film. It only cost $38 million to remind Depp’s Scrooge of the Christmas spirit. “Ebenezer” has also earned $45.9 million internationally, bringing its global total to a respectable $78.4 million.

The film is only showing in 35mm, which limits the number of screenings available to cinephiles and PTA completists.

#3391. 5 Greatest YA Movie Franchises Of All Time, Ranked

Young adult stories have always made for compelling movie adaptations, especially when you look at the massive YA movie boom that began in the early 2000s. Magical worlds, dystopian futures, complicated love triangles, and the supernatural surrounding various coming-of-age stories will always have strong entertainment potential, though some are better than others.

The very best YA movie franchises turn relatable and familiar coming-of-age experiences into major cinematic experiences, balancing honoring the source material with offering new perspectives at the same time. As such, it's notable that our choices for the top five greatest YA movie franchises are all still ongoing with brand-new projects in some form or another, from Harry Potter to The Hunger Games.

This ranking will consider a few different key factors, including overall quality, consistency, how well it adapts and expands the source material, world-building, and cultural impact. Keeping that in mind, here are the five greatest YA movie franchises ranked from great to greatest.

Disney and 20th Century Fox's Chronicles of Narnia movies brought C.S. Lewis' beloved fantasy novels to life, starting with 2005's The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe. Audiences were introduced to the Pevensie children who discover the magical land of Narnia and ultimately join the fight against the White Witch.

Without question, the first movie remains the peak of the franchise, though 2008's Prince Caspian offered a compelling darker journey with the Pevensies' return to a very different Narnia. 2010's Voyage of the Dawn Treader also adapted the source material fairly well. However, the franchise lost momentum and stalled after the third film, so much so that the rest of the books in Lewis' series were never adapted in this iteration of the franchise. That's a large reason why this ranks so low on this list, despite still being one of the GOATs.

Looking ahead, it will be very interesting to see how Netflix and Greta Gerwig's The Magician's Nephew fares next year, a brand-new take on the franchise that looks to be incredibly unique.

DreamWorks' How to Train Your Dragon franchise is one of the most emotionally satisfying animated movie sagas ever made, with its focus on a young outcast Viking named Hiccup and a dragon named Toothless. Managing to change his entire village's hatred of dragons, the franchise gets better with every entry as Hiccup gradually evolves into a great leader and hero for his people.

There's an incredibly rich coming-of-age story baked into the entire franchise that is also full of some of the greatest dragon designs and animated action sequences of all time (not to mention one of the very best movie scores as well). Having expanded into television, short films, and most recently the start of a whole live-action adaptation, the enduring popularity and audience engagement are a clear testament to its GOAT status, though here's hoping the rest of the live-action franchise lives up to its animated counterparts as the first movie did.

It may not yet have the same cultural footprint as the top three from a live-action standpoint, but it still delivers one of the most satisfying and complete narratives on this list.

Speaking of cultural impact, few YA movie franchises have had quite as big an impact as Twilight. Based on Stephenie Meyer's bestselling novels, the supernatural romance series saw Bella Swan falling in love with Edward Cullen, a vampire struggling between his own feelings for her and his more dangerous impulses. The series only expands from there, featuring a love triangle with werewolves (Jacob), rival vampires, and major supernatural political conflicts.

Running from 2008–2012, the five-film Twilight franchise was a huge cultural phenomenon that is still talked about today, particularly as the key franchise that helped launch Robert Pattinson's ongoing stardom as one of the biggest stars today (who else has ever played Batman and James Bond simultaneously?) The Twilight saga also inspired several other YA movie romance adaptations and supernatural stories. Despite the inconsistency between films and major melodrama throughout, its cultural impact and massive fanbase can't be dismissed.

Suzanne Collins' The Hunger Games novels became one of the most compelling YA movie franchises of the 2010s. Set in the dystopian nation of Panem created from the ashes of what was North America, the main four-film series focuses on Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence), who volunteers to take her younger sister's place in a televised battle to the death, featuring children randomly selected from each of the nation's 12 districts for the entertainment of the wealthy elite living in the Capitol.

Following her survival in the first book/movie along with Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson), what follows is Katniss' evolution into a major symbol of revolution known as the Mockingjay as the nation falls into civil war, examining the power of propaganda, class inequality, political manipulation and corruption, and the cost of revolution itself (there's also a major love triangle).

Running from 2012-2015, the original four-film Hunger Games series provided an incredibly satisfying adaptation of Collins' primary trilogy, with Catching Fire standing out as a very strong sequel. However, the franchise has since continued with 2023's The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, exploring the younger years of President Snow, while Sunrise on the Reaping has just been released this year and is now playing in theaters, starring a young Haymitch Abernathy and more legacy characters in a major prequel revealing the events of the second Quarter Quell.

Both spin-off prequels prove the ongoing narrative potential of the world of Panem and The Hunger Games as one of the strongest YA movie franchises ever...aside from one that absolutely holds the top spot.

It truly is difficult to imagine any YA movie franchise surpassing Warner Bros.' Harry Potter films. Beginning with 2001's The Sorcerer's Stone, audiences were introduced to a magical world and school for witchcraft and wizardry that is endlessly captivating and full of wonder, even as the eight-film series evolves into a major magical war against the dark forces of Voldemort.

Few cinematic trios are as beloved as Harry, Ron, and Hermione, and even fewer have been given as much time to grow and evolve on-screen across 10 years of storytelling. Likewise, Harry Potter's incredibly consistent cast throughout those 10 years is a huge advantage for the franchise. By all accounts, the main Harry Potter saga is one of the most emotionally satisfying journeys in all of cinema (Forget just YA movie franchises).

Beyond the original saga, the ongoing potential of the Wizarding World was shown with the Fantastic Beasts prequel series. Despite its mixed results, the films still maintained high fan engagement and added to the franchise's overall cultural impact.

Looking ahead, Warner Bros is set to release its new Harry Potter streaming series on HBO Max at the end of the year, a full reboot with an all-new cast that intends to adapt one book per season. On the one hand, it's a testament to the original movie franchise and its enduring cultural impact as a huge piece of IP. On the other, the Harry Potter movies are still so beloved that trying to reboot the franchise is a massive risk and is already facing controversies ahead of its premiere this Christmas.

At any rate, Harry Potter's iconic world-building, memorable performances, and extraordinary cultural influence all serve to make it the most complete and greatest YA franchise on this list. More than any other YA series, Harry Potter made audiences feel like they were essentially growing up alongside its heroes. As a result, it's highly doubtful there will ever be a bigger GOAT when it comes to YA movie franchises.

Harry Potter is a multimedia franchise about an orphaned boy who enrolls at Hogwarts School of Wizardry, where he learns the truth about himself, his family, and the terrible evil that haunts the magical world. Adapted from the novels, Harry Potter is an eight-episode film saga that follows the journey of Harry Potter and his friends, Hermoine Granger and Ron Weasley, as they navigate the tricky world of growing up, school life, and magic. Starting from year one and moving to their seventh year, the films chronicle the students' time at Hogwarts while unfurling a sinister plot that centers around the unsuspecting Harry. With the return of the dark wizard, Voldemort, the students and professors at Hogwarts will fight to carry on as the world around them may change forever. Harry Potter has expanded beyond the world of its films and novels with several video games, a spin-off film series titled Fantastic Beasts, and even attractions at Universal Studios.

#3390. 10 Books Like ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ You Should Read Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

There’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth. (Did I mention he's accompanied by his ex-girlfriend’s suddenly talkative cat?)

The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.

An isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone). He has magic that works like a video game, and has to deal with quests that slowly give him clothes (it’s a relief when he finally acquires some pants), force him to survive cannibals, and hunt down various monsters that definitely need killing. It’s got the same “gaming rules” structure as DCC and a similarly absurdist tone, with just the right spice of darkness.

The Cradle series by Will Wight isn’t a LitRPG, and it doesn’t have Carl’s focus on humor, but it’s another progression fantasy with enough game-like elements to be a great match. Lindon is an “unsouled,” incapable of gaining any of the sacred arts and doomed to a life without a future. His lack of power makes Lindon ferociously determined to find an alternative path to power and success, and that’s what drives this story. He has to find creative ways to move forward, and slowly this leads him to a path that just might make him the most powerful person in his world. DCC fans will love the progression and the tone.

One of the key elements of any video game is the respawn—you get killed, but you pop back up to try again, sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at a save point. Django Wexler leverages that mechanic to great effect in How to Become the Dark Lord and Die Trying. Davi has been summoned to a fantasy world to be the hero, the person who defeats the Dark Lord and saves the day—but she’s failed (and died) so many times, she’s fed up, and decides that on this run through, she’s going to switch sides and become the Dark Lord, using all her knowledge gained from endless replays to her advantage. The humor is pitch-black the way DCC fans like it, and the progressive structure is a perfect fit.

Is Princess Donut your favorite part of Dungeon Crawler Carl? Of course she is. In that case, check out Andrew Seiple’s Threadbare series. Threadbare is a stuffed bear brought to magical life in a failed experiment. He’s a foot tall, full of stuffing, and extremely dumb when the story begins. But when he’s rescued by a little girl and plunged into a horrible series of dangers, Threadbare has to find a way to level up. Like DCC, Threadbare starts off leaning into the absurdity and humor, then slowly gains emotional gravitas as the story progresses.

If you play tabletop RPGs, you’ve encountered a Murderhobo or two: A character who solves all their problems by killing—even members of their own party. Luke doesn’t aspire to be a Murderhobo—he just wants to take over the family business and hang with his buddies. But when an invasion threatens the kingdom, everyone over the age of 17 is ordered to be tested for Potential. Luke’s friends all test high and join the Ascender Corps, traveling to different planes for training. Luke tests ... very low, and when he steps through a portal to engage in his training, he finds himself without any guidance or training in a strange, deadly world where his only chance of survival is to murder his way through it. It’s dark, darkly funny, and a progression fantasy like no other.

If you’re looking for a book series that combines the dark, chaotic humor, absurd game mechanics, and surprising emotional depth of Carl, here’s Ryan “Quicksave” Romano, a man who has the unique ability to literally create a save point in his existence that allows him to go back and redo things whenever he dies. Searching for a childhood friend, he becomes embroiled in a violent gang war that lets him make good use of his power—but underneath the snark and the insanity of Ryan’s existence is a surprisingly affecting story of a man who has suffered, and suffered countless tragedies that are definitely taking their toll.

If your fave bit of DCC is Carl himself—a mediocre dude in an extraordinary situation—you should read Dennis E. Taylor’s fantastic Bobiverse books. Bob is a software engineer who hits it big and promptly dies, waking up to discover a century has passed and he’s been repurposed as an AI controlling a space probe searching for new planets for humanity to inhabit. If he fails in his mission (and he’s not the only probe out there), he’ll be turned off for good. Luckily, he can make copies of himself, and he’s pretty smart. The humor here is smart and soaked in pop culture, making it a perfect match for DCC fans.

Want more of Carl’s absurdist humor? Mayor of Noobtown is the LitRPG you’re looking for. Jim dies and wakes up in a video game-esque universe and finds himself stuck in the zone designated for newbies—players with no experience, skill, or hope. The area fell out of the mainline progression mechanic a long time ago, so there doesn’t seem to be a way to gain power, and the monsters are not at all concerned about the unfairness of it all, so Jim has to figure out how to advance in a universe that seems designed to kill him (again).

If you want to lean into the meta side of things, check out Scathing Reviewer, written by an author who goes by the unusual pen name "BananaDragon." Liu Peijin is the author of a sprawling LitRPG web novel, and she’s used to the bad reviews and complaints from readers—and quite combative about it. When her books’ universe blossoms into a very dangerous new reality, she should be perfectly positioned to survive, having written the story in the first place. But her story becoming real also means her insufferable protagonist is real, and all those nasty critics are now passing judgment on her entire existence. It’s a dark, funny takedown of the entire genre itself, and DCC fans will love it.

If you want a story that parallels the dungeon crawling aspect of DCC, Andrew Rowe’s Arcane Ascension series is the ticket. The Serpent Spire is a tower of constantly changing traps, puzzles, and dangerous creatures. If you enter and survive, you emerge with magical powers. Corin Cadence’s brother entered the Serpent Spire years ago and never returned—and now Corin is determined not only to survive, but to make it to the top, where legend says a goddess will grant you whatever you wish. And what Corin wants is his brother back. It’s a literal progression combined with LitRPG rules, game-inspired puzzle-solving, and a complex magic system that fans of Carl will definitely enjoy.

#3389. Rian Johnson Leaves the Door Open to Star Wars Return: ‘It’s a World I Deeply Love’

Rian Johnson isn’t writing a Star Wars movie, but he isn’t ruling one out, either.

Responding to a question from IndieWire during an in-conversation event at the 23rd Marrakech International Film Festival, the writer/director of “Star Wars: The Last Jedi” was clear that his next project lies elsewhere: “I’m already writing the next thing I’m going to do, and it’s not a Star Wars thing, or in that genre,” he said.

“I’m very much enjoying just making my own stuff, but I mean, if the opportunity presented itself,” Johnson said, nodding. “It’s a world I deeply love. It’s also a group of people I love.”

“I love Star Wars more now than I ever have,” he added. “And it’s exciting to me that there are a lot of different voices now taking cracks at it.” The timing is hard to ignore. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Debuts to Mighty $120 Million, Reviving Lionsgate’s Most Important Franchise Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Crosses $100 Million Globally

Johnson’s remarks land just as Lucasfilm appears to be turning back toward the corner of the saga he helped shape. Polygon reported that two long-gestating features, “Star Wars: New Jedi Order” and an untitled film from Dave Filoni, are still listed as in development by Production Weekly, despite months of silence and the soft box office performance of “The Mandalorian & Grogu.”

“New Jedi Order” would theoretically bring back actress Daisy Ridley as Rey roughly 15 years after “The Rise of Skywalker,” rebuilding the Jedi Order that “The Last Jedi” so memorably called into question. Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy is attached to direct, with George Nolfi now writing after earlier drafts from Damon Lindelof and Justin Britt-Gibson, and a stint by Bond 26 screenwriter Steven Knight. The film was pulled from its December 17, 2027 release date in May 2025. Meanwhile, “Star Wars: Starfighter,” the Shawn Levy-directed film starring Ryan Gosling and set five years after “The Rise of Skywalker,” remains the only Star Wars feature with a firm date: May 28, 2027.

In 2017, the year “The Last Jedi” hit theaters, Lucasfilm announced that Johnson would create a new Star Wars trilogy. Those films have yet to materialize, but Johnson had warm words for Filoni, who took on the role of Lucasfilm’s president and chief creative officer in January: “Dave Filoni I got to know while making ‘The Last Jedi’, and he’s a wonderful guy who really has the spirit of Star Wars in him,” he said. “All the Lucasfilm folks are awesome.”

Later, answering questions from the audience, Johnson described “The Last Jedi” as “the most joyful process of any movie I’ve ever made”, despite the challenge of stepping from his own original films into what he called a contested mythology.

“I’m a huge, huge fan of George Lucas, and I’ve read a lot about when he was writing the original Star Wars, how personal it was for him,” Johnson continued. “I think especially with something that has a deep cultural impact, and that belongs to everybody, that makes it even more important… to make sure it’s coming from a personal perspective and something that’s deeply on fire inside you, as opposed to thinking, ‘what’s gonna please this person and this person and this person’. That leads to homogeneity, to repeating yourself and to something that feels dead on screen.”

As a middle chapter, “The Last Jedi” drew directly on Johnson’s childhood experience of “The Empire Strikes Back,” though not as something to copy. “I didn’t want to imitate ‘The Empire Strikes Back’,” Johnson said. “What I wanted to get to was the heart of what that movie has, which is this center part of life where your job is to fail, and your job is to learn from that and to get up and keep moving forward.”

He drew a distinction between a film having a moral compass and having a moral. The compass, he said, “comes from the entire mass of every single creative decision made by the writer, or director, or whole team.”

Johnson also reflected on the only two composers he has worked with. His cousin Nathan Johnson has scored his films since the pair started making movies together at age ten: “Nathan is the first person to read the script; he’s on set for the entire shoot so it’s very much a collaboration.”

John Williams, he said, is also “a miracle of a human being”, and working with him was the opposite experience. “You give him the movie and then the first time I hear any music is when we’re on the scoring stage, and there are 200 musicians playing it.”

If Johnson does return to Star Wars, it seems he won’t be thinking about franchise strategy. “For me it’s not about thinking about IP, it’s about stories,” he said. “I deeply believe the only way to actually make a movie that matters and is worth something is to have your eyes nowhere else except on making that movie. What is the story we’re telling? Why are we telling it? Why do we care about it?”

“Outside of that bubble,” Johnson added, “I’ll leave it to the executives.”

With those executives now steering Star Wars back toward Rey and the post-“Rise of Skywalker” era, the bubble may be closer to his than it has been in years.

#3387. Hogwarts Legacy 2 Official Release Update Issued By Warner Bros

Despite the controversy surrounding its launch, there is no denying that Hogwarts Legacy dominated the gaming sphere in 2023, with the Harry Potter-inspired RPG even going on to become the best-selling game of the year.

As such, it was not long before a sequel was announced, and over the past three years, Avalanche Software has been hard at work getting ready to send players back to Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry.

It may have been the best-selling game of 2023, but Hogwarts Legacy did not come without its downfalls, especially as it did not receive any expansions or substantial post-game content drops. As such, fans are feeling mixed over a sequel. Will it expand on the open-world and offer long-term content, or will it be much of the same?

At the time of writing, Hogwarts Legacy 2 does not have a release date, or even a release window, despite previous rumors suggesting that it would coincide with the upcoming launch of the Harry Potter television show, which is set to debut on Christmas Day. However, it is unlikely that Hogwarts Legacy 2 is going to pop up over the next month, so we can safely assume that it will be 2027 at the earliest.

It was back in October that Warner Bros., the publishers behind Hogwarts Legacy, issued a statement on the game's progress, and after Paramount acquired Warner Bros. Discovery, it was confirmed that Warner Bros. Games would merge with Paramount Games Studio to create one giant gaming division.

It will be this gaming division that works on Hogwarts Legacy 2, but, as mentioned, no further information has been revealed, and fans are yet to see any gameplay or substantial updates. As such, its potential cancellation has been a subject of worry for fans, but according to a letter to shareholders discussing WB's games division, WB's strategy will be to focus on its most successful franchises, with Harry Potter being one of them. "We expect Games to more meaningfully contribute to segment profitability going forward as our pipeline expands," the statement reads, "including the second installment of Hogwarts Legacy."

With The Game Awards taking place on December 10, we can only hope that this next major gaming event will spare a moment for Hogwarts Legacy 2, and it would be perfect timing in the lead-up to the Harry Potter television show, especially as the two projects are rumored to be working together closely. However, this is mere speculation, and for now, we will have to wait with bated breath to see what comes next for the franchise.

Back in 2023, our very own William Cennamo awarded Hogwarts Legacy an almost perfect 9/10, with his review reading:

Hogwarts Legacy is a wonderful game filled to the brim with adventures to be had, activities to engage in, and secrets to be found. The school and the surrounding areas have been recreated beautifully, and players will easily lose hours lost in the whimsical splendor of this wizarding world.

Amazon's early Black Friday 2026 sale is already bringing substantial discounts to smart TVs, with savings ranging from $200 to $1,350 across models from Samsung, LG, Hisense, Sony, TCL, and other major brands. Several of the TVs included are from this year's lineups, so you don't necessarily have to settle for an older model to get a good price. There's also a decent variety to choose from, whether you're looking for an OLED TV with excellent contrast for movie nights, a bright mini-LED display for a sunlit living room, or simply a bigger screen without spending a fortune.

We've rounded up some of the more interesting offers below, and you can check out the rest of our Black Friday coverage for more editor-vetted tech deals as the sale continues.

Samsung’s 65-inch S90H is down to $1,397.99 from $1,897.99, saving you $500 on the company’s mid-range OLED TV for 2026. It’s a solid option for movie enthusiasts and gamers alike, thanks to its self-lit pixels that produce deep blacks and excellent contrast, particularly in darker scenes where conventional LED TVs can struggle with a grayish glow. You also get a high-refresh-rate display for smoother gaming.

If you have room for a bigger screen, Samsung’s 77-inch S85H is also worth a look, especially now that it’s down to $1,797.99 from $2,197.99, saving you $400. Although it sits below the S90H in Samsung’s 2026 OLED lineup, it still delivers the deep blacks, excellent contrast, and wide viewing angles that make OLED TVs appealing. The larger screen also makes it a good fit for family movie nights.

One of the biggest discounts in this roundup, the 2026 75-inch Hisense U7 is now $997.99, down from $1,999.99. Its mini-LED backlighting and local dimming are designed to deliver brighter highlights and better contrast, making it an appealing option for rooms with plenty of natural light. Gaming-focused features also make it worth a look if you plan to connect a current-generation console or gaming PC.

For a more affordable 75-inch option, Hisense's 2026 U6 Pro is down to $699.99 from $1,399.99, saving you $700. Like the U7, it uses mini-LED backlighting to improve contrast and bring out more detail in HDR movies and shows, although it sits a tier below the U7 in terms of overall picture performance. It also comes with Fire TV and Alexa+ built in, making it a convenient choice for households already using Amazon's smart home ecosystem.

The C6 is LG’s mid-range OLED evo model for 2026, and right now its 65-inch model is $1,399.99, down from its $2,699.99 launch price. It combines excellent pixel-level contrast with gaming features designed for fast-paced titles, making it a versatile choice for both movies and consoles. LG also supports Dolby Vision, which gives it an advantage over Samsung's OLEDs for viewers who regularly stream compatible HDR content.

Sony’s 65-inch Bravia 6, the entry-level OLED in its 2026 TV lineup, is now $1,198, down from $1,999.99, saving you $802. It delivers the deep blacks and excellent contrast you'd expect from the display technology, thanks to its self-lit pixels. Sony's picture processing also helps bring out fine details and natural-looking colors in movies and TV shows, while Dolby Vision support makes the most of compatible HDR content.

For the same $1,198, you can get a considerably larger screen with the 85-inch Sony Bravia 3 II, which is down from $1,599.99, saving you $402. That said, this 2026 model uses a conventional LED panel, so it won't quite match the Bravia 6's deep blacks and contrast, but the extra 20 inches make it an appealing option for sports and family movie nights. It also has a native 120Hz refresh rate with VRR and ALLM for smoother console gaming, along with Dolby Vision support and Google TV with Gemini built in.

Toshiba’s 75-inch Z670R is down to $699.99 from $1,299.99, saving you $600 on a 2026 mini-LED TV. It combines full-array local dimming with QLED color technology for improved contrast and brighter highlights, while Toshiba’s REGZA Engine ZRi processor helps sharpen lower-resolution content. The native 144Hz refresh rate also makes it a good option for console and PC gaming, and you get Fire TV built in for streaming, along with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos support.

It's a 4K QLED TV, with a native 165Hz refresh rate, built-in Fire TV, and the same REGZA Engine ZRi processor found in the Z670R. But there's more to it than watching movies and shows, as its Ambient Mode can display over 3,000 curated artworks without a subscription, while the matte anti-glare screen and included white oak frame help it pass for a framed print on the wall.

TCL’s 98-inch F8D is down to $1,444.99 from $1,699.99, saving you $255 on a massive 2026 QLED Fire TV. It uses a high-brightness LED backlight, so you won't get the same level of contrast control as TCL's more expensive mini-LED QM models, but it still offers a native 144Hz refresh rate for smoother gaming, along with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos support. And at nearly 100 inches, there's plenty of screen space to make movies, sports, and games feel more immersive.

It also runs the same Roku OS found on the company’s streaming sticks and comes with an Enhanced Voice Remote, so navigating apps and finding something to watch should feel familiar to anyone who already uses Roku.

There's no guarantee that Cyber Monday will bring lower TV prices, particularly when some of the early Black Friday deals are already offering discounts approaching 50%. That depends on your budget, room size, and how you plan to use it. For a large screen at a relatively affordable price, the 75-inch Hisense U6 Pro at $699.99 stands out, while the 65-inch Roku Plus Series at $449.99 makes sense for everyday streaming on a tighter budget. If screen size is your priority, the 98-inch TCL F8D is also worth a look, provided you have the room for it.

Now, whilst we wait to see how it all ends, Game of Thrones: Dragonfire is set to take us back to the beginning as a much younger Rhaenyra Targaryen returns to the fray.

First launching back in June of this year, Game of Thrones: Dragonfire is an Android and iOS 4X strategy and role-playing game developed by Warner Bros. Games. "Headstrong and fiercely intelligent, Rhaenyra rides the dragon Syrax and has grown up in the shadow of the Iron Throne. The smallfolk of King’s Landing call her “the Realm’s Delight,” though the great lords whisper that a woman’s claim, however strong in blood, may yet be tested by men who will not suffer a queen.”

#3383. OpenAI upgrades ChatGPT and Codex with new GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol models

OpenAI kicked off the GPT-6 generation with Astra in September, then upgraded Sol to GPT-6.1 a few weeks later at DevDay.

Today, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol are coming to ChatGPT Work and Codex together. OpenAI says both can finish demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you can get more done before hitting your usage limit.

Astra is still the model OpenAI recommends for your hardest projects.

Say you have a screenshot of a slide and want the rest of your presentation to look like it. OpenAI says GPT-6.2 Astra can use that screenshot as a template and match the layout, colors, and even the font size.

On the Codex side, OpenAI says Astra is better at making and testing changes in an existing project.

“Early testers reported cleaner code style and more focused tests, with fewer rounds of revision,” OpenAI says.

Sol is the more affordable model for everyday coding and writing, and it gets surprisingly close to Astra on one coding test.

Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 measures whether changes to real codebases are good enough for maintainers to merge.

With both models at maximum reasoning effort, OpenAI says Sol came within half a point of Astra at about one-fifth the cost.

Some of you have been asking very politely. Some of you have just been asking.GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are now available.Super efficient and built to perform where it counts—the real world.https://t.co/qr2iP0GpfX pic.twitter.com/jLCyVIws2Y

Both models are available starting today in ChatGPT Work and Codex on Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu.

The $200/month Pro plan also gets Ultrafast mode for the first time with Sol. The $500/month Pro plan gets Ultrafast on both models, as do eligible Enterprise and Edu workspaces once an admin enables it.

How fast is Ultrafast? OpenAI says it can generate tokens at up to 4.5 times the standard rate on either model, although it uses more of your allowance. You can switch speeds from the model picker.

Developers can use both models through the API today as well. Astra’s standard input and output prices are 20% lower than with GPT-6 Astra, while Sol keeps its GPT-6.1 pricing.

You can read more in OpenAI’s full announcement.

#3382. Forget ‘Twilight,’ Netflix’s 6-Season Series Is Leaving Streaming

The YA supernatural genre gained its popularity due to the global success of Twilight. Fans around the world found themselves fascinated by the existence of vampires and werewolves, eagerly wanting more monster content for young adult audiences. A slew of new shows and movies released in the years after Twilight. The Vampire Diaries, True Blood, and The Originals gave viewers similar content to enjoy, but one show focused on the underrated side that Twilight didn't share enough about.

Teen Wolf truly feels like its own story. Loosely based off the 1985 film of the same name, starring Michael J. Fox, the show takes the story in countless unique directions. When Scott (Tyler Posey) is bitten by a werewolf, his whole life changes in a single moment, and he finds himself thrown into a world full of supernatural threats, dangerous endeavors, and unlikely allies. The show feels reminiscent of other supernatural media of the time, but doesn't limit itself to the mold Twilight created.

Twilight centers around the existence of vampires with werewolves serving as secondary supernatural forces. While werewolves are present in the saga, they aren't fully explored in the same way vampires are. Instead of focusing on vampires, Teen Wolf breaks from the mold and dedicates itself wholly to exploring what becoming a werewolf is like. The show feels like it could be from Jacob Black's (Taylor Lautner) perspective as a werewolf. Balancing high school and the experience of being a supernatural creature is truly explored in this show, giving audiences a look into what further development into Jacob's werewolf experience might have been like.

As Twilight centers heavily on vampires, the werewolves often feel less developed or focused on. Jacob is reduced to an alternative option within Bella's love triangle. Teen Wolf gives attention to werewolves in a way that Twilight would have benefited from. Scott could be seen as a version of Jacob that fans never got to see, giving them a glimpse into another side of Jacob's character that could have been explored.

In every generation, there is an iconic line that changes history.

As he withholds the truth of his double life from his family and friends, Scott's personal life becomes very complicated. His friendships become embroiled in his werewolf activities, often pushing his friends too far as they try to stop supernatural threats. Scott's relationship with Allison is directly impacted by his transformation. Audiences rooted for the pair to get together, but when they did, new challenges arose that viewers and Scott weren't expecting. Allison's family and hunting background presents a direct and personal danger that Scott has to skirt around.

Outside his personal life, Scott finds himself thrown into the middle of a supernatural disaster. With his town serving as a beacon for paranormal activities, Scott becomes a protector of his town. The weight of the role impacts Scott and puts real pressure onto this young character who never expected to be a hero. As he grows in his own abilities, Scott finds a way to haphazardly balance his two lives, but it's never the same as before. Becoming a werewolf isn't an easy transition, and the show doesn't shy away from all the issues Scott deals with after being bitten.

Teen Wolf could have followed in Twilight's footsteps. It would have taken the easy route and presented Twilight with some small alterations, but the show decided to push further. The series introduces new monsters and threats that keep the show feeling unique and unlike anything else in the YA supernatural genre. Its intense plot lines and myriad of entertaining characters make for the perfect binge for fans of Twilight looking for more werewolf content.

#3379. Assassin's Creed: Echoes Of The Past Officially Releasing December 2026

Since the launch of Assassin's Creed in 2007, the stealth-action series from Ubisoft has become one of the cornerstones of gaming, and with fourteen mainline entries now under its belt, it is safe to say that it is here to stay.

Taking players across the globe, and exploring multiple eras, movements, and cultures, Assassin's Creed has been the best history teacher we could have had, and to celebrate the franchise approaching its 20th anniversary, Assassin's Creed: Echoes of the Past is set to stun us all when it arrives this December.

Courtesy of the artist collective Les 7 Doigts, Heredis: Echoes of the Past is a live show that takes fans to the Ubisoft universe with an experience that combines both theater and circus. Oh, and of course, there will also be plenty of parkour.

Whilst a preview will be held on 3 December 2026, at the Maisonneuve Theater in Montreal, several performances will be scheduled between January 21 and February 7, 2027, and so you have plenty of time to grab your tickets. So, what can you expect?

A troop of acrobats will take to the stage to perform some incredible stunts, with the show itself expected to last two hours. However, the storyline will focus on a young man called Naël who, after receiving a letter on his 25th birthday, will find his destiny changed forever. As such, he will have to embark on a journey to discover the mystery behind his father's appearance, an event that he refuses to accept.

Featuring an original Assassin's Creed storyline, Heredis: Echoes of the Past will see Naël join the HEREDIS program, and through this, he will be able to travel through many historical eras which echo the ones we all know and love from the Assassin's Creed franchise so far. Not only that, but with the stage show being officially supported by Ubisoft, you can expect a truly spectacular experience with the creator's stamp of approval.

Despite featuring nods to the games, such as in the historical periods that are covered, it will not focus on any of the games. As such, even those unfamiliar with the franchise will be able to go and watch. However, the catch here is that, unless you can make the Montreal preview, you will need to head to the Casino de Paris, France.

Over on r/assassinscreed, fans discussed the upcoming stage show, and took to the comments to share their thoughts. One user shared, "One of the theater companies I work with presented one of 7Fingers’ shows a year or so before I started working there, and they were pretty well-attended shows. We are thinking of bringing them back to present another of their works, hopefully in the next few years. I really hope 7Fingers is able to bring Heredis to more than just Canada and France!" Another shared, "This actually sounds incredible to be honest."

So, if you find yourself in Canada or France and just so happen to be an Assassin's Creed fan, make sure to check out Heredis: Echoes of the Past and partake in an original experience you will never forget.

#3377. Josh Holloway Steals the 'Tracker' Show From Colter Shaw | Review

Tracker may have outdone itself this week by pairing Colter Shaw (Justin Hartley) with an unlikely ally who couldn't be more different from our hero on paper. "That's The Job" brings newcomer Josh Holloway into the picture as bounty hunter/gun-for-hire Luke Kelso, who finds himself on the wrong side of Colter's latest job. Just after our favorite rewardist united with his entire cast last week, the CBS program introduces a one-off character who we hope to see again.

This week's episode picks up in Gray Haven, South Carolina, where bed and breakfast owner John Iddo (Tinpo Lee) closes everything down for the night. However, upon seeing someone outside, he goes out to investigate, only to be suddenly attacked. The next day, Colter is on the road when he gets a call from his latest flame, Jenna Nova (Gillian Bolt), who is on a job collecting a vintage car with her father, Mario (Daniel Edward Mora). The pair rapid-fire some banter about drinks and darts, reminding us why this pair work so well together. It's a sweet little moment as Colter pulls into his next job, and quite the juxtaposition with how the episode ends. Arriving at the B&B, Colter speaks with Eliza (Ruby Jay), John's employee and daughter figure who is concerned about his disappearance. Colter presses her to tell him everything, and Eliza reveals that he takes sleeping pills for insomnia. Walking outside, he finds some blood and evidence of a struggle, as well as what looks like a kill switch for a water sports vehicle. It's then that Eliza reveals that John had gotten into a recent confrontation with some jet ski guys who may have stolen credit card information from B&B guests.

Tracker works because the case changes every week and the four people solving it never do. Here is which of them you are, what it says about you, and the case for yours being the best of the four.

You would rather handle it yourself and you are usually capable of doing so. Colter is a survivalist who lives in an Airstream and takes reward money for finding missing people, which is a premise that only works because he is clearly running from something of his own.

You know somebody, and that somebody owes you a favour. Reenie is the lawyer Colter calls when a case needs a door opened legally, and she is the only person on the show who can get further with a phone call than he can on foot.

You are two steps ahead and you rarely mention it. Bobby is the one who finds the thing that unlocks the case, usually from a desk, usually about ninety seconds before anybody realises they needed it.

You turn up, change the temperature of the room, and leave people arguing about you. Russell is Colter's brother, ex-military, and the show has never once let the audience settle on whether he is a help or a problem, which is exactly why he keeps coming back.

When Colter goes to confront the parties responsible, he finds himself surrounded by two guys — which really just means that they're outnumbered. Colter pushes back, pinning one of the jet ski bums and pressing him for more information about John. He’s told that another employee, Lenny Remy (Dylan Kenin), is the man to talk to. Apparently, Lenny went by John's place to send a message, but they hadn’t heard from him since. So, Colter calls Randy (Chris Lee), and it seems like Lenny is bad news. The tech whiz sends our hero to the last pinged location: a trailer park on the other side of town. Entering a condemned manufactured home, Colter finds Lenny beaten and tied up in the closet. According to Lenny, “some psycho” beat him up after he attacked John, knocking him out before he woke up there. When Lenny finally came to, he heard an argument between John and the mystery man — this was a few hours ago. That mystery man? None other than Josh Holloway's Luke, who drops John off at some location after telling him none of it is personal.

Colter continues to look around and finds a few security cameras nearby. Typically, this is when he dials Randy and gets all the footage he needs, but according to Tracker's resident tech guru, it appears that the camera went blank for an hour or so. Colter theorizes that the hired man ran a jammer, which Randy discovers came from a laptop, which is then tracked to the local Dogwood Motel. When Colter arrives, he breaks into a nearby room next to Luke, who readies a firearm of his own. After blasting through the door, Colter narrowly avoids being shot. The man runs, and Colter follows. The result is probably the best fight sequence we've seen this season, maybe on the show period, before Colter gets Luke to talk. From what the bounty hunter knows, he simply dropped John off at a lawyer's office. With the police on the way, Luke decides to go with Colter, albeit as more of a prisoner than a partner.

As Luke soon reveals, he was paid $100K to grab John and not ask questions. This leads to a quick debate over the ethics of their respective professions, where Luke eventually reveals that John’s real name isn't John at all. Rather, he was told that he was really David Watanabe, a man who previously harmed the lawyer in question by supposedly ripping off a Japanese hotel, killing a man, and escaping to the United States. This rattles Colter a little, but a phone call from Reenie (Fiona Rene) puts all the facts back in order. As it turns out, John didn’t kill anyone at all, but rather saved a woman from her abusive husband, Hiro Tanaka (Sonny Saito). After the ex-wife, Mika (Chika Kanamoto), escaped, she turned over evidence of Hiro’s crimes, sending him to prison for decades. Now that Hiro is back, he's itching for revenge.

Colter returns to the Lone Star State for a new mystery.

Although unsure about it at first, Luke eventually agrees to help Colter, who tells him that he needs to make things right. Upon arriving at Hiro's offices, they head inside to find the place empty. It seems as if, after Luke delivered John to the former gangster, he took him and ran. They even find John’s fingernails ripped off and littered on the floor. At this point, it seems as if the pair have hit a dead end, only for Tracker to lay down the tragedy quite thickly this week. After Colter notices a broken lock to a nearby dumpster, they find John dead inside. Although Luke at first wants to take a step back from it all, Colter gives him a choice: either let John die for nothing or use this to help him find and save Mika. Of course, Colter's heroic charm is quite convincing, and Luke agrees to help, tracing Hiro’s number to a local library.

At the library, Mika closes up for the night only to be surrounded by Hiro and his men. The criminal reveals that he killed John, only for Mika to fight back, killing one of the two goons and escaping into the nearby bookshelves. It isn't long before Colter and Luke arrive, splitting up to cover more ground. This was the right call, as Hiro corners Mika, ready to deliver the final blow when Luke stops him. Unfortunately, Hiro gets a shot off and wounds Luke pretty bad — but before he can finish the job, Colter shoots the gangster dead and stabilizes his newfound partner. With all this fast-paced gunplay, we need to get Colter, Luke, and Jensen Ackles' Russell Shaw in a room.

The next day, Colter runs into Mika at the hospital, who stuck around to thank Luke when he woke up — it turns out that the bounty hunter is out of surgery and is in recovery. Colter dips in to check on Luke, who wonders if our favorite rewardist has a "walk-away number" when it comes to the job. Of course, Colter doesn't. “I like what I do,” he explains. “I like fixing things. I like bringing people back together.” For Colter, the job gives him purpose and others hope, and so, despite all the profit he makes, it’s never been about the money. But "That's The Job" doesn't end here. True to the title, Colter now has to go and do the hard thing by informing Eliza about John's death, and it's a heartfelt, intimate moment that reminds us that, sometimes, not even Colter Shaw can bring about a happy ending.

Tracker goes beyond Colter Shaw's abilities as he partners with an unlikely ally to see things through.

#3376. Why iPhone Duo wasn’t for me (but might be for you)

I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it. Here are the three main reasons why the Duo didn’t work out for me, but might for you.

I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands. You can use it one-handed, but for me it’s not nearly as comfortable as the iPhone 18 Pro. It’s too wide and too heavy to be used for long.

Perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions. But that would be a pretty significant shift for me, as there are so many situations when I don’t have both hands free.

If you already use two hands with your iPhone regularly—perhaps because you have a Pro Max model—then the Duo’s one-handed experience likely won’t bother you. But the more I used the Duo, the more I found myself missing my iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest value proposition of a foldable is that it’s a 2-in-1 product, letting you have a standard phone but also a tablet-sized display that fits in your pocket.

I totally get the appeal, and fully expected to love that hybrid design. But after two weeks of trying, I still struggled to find times when I actually wanted to unfold the Duo. And to be clear, that’s a me problem, not an issue with the Duo itself.

I tried a bunch of apps on the inner display, and struggled to find use cases that—for me—made it worthwhile to open the Duo. But based on the feedback I’ve seen from most Duo owners, I’m very much in the minority.

I know lots of people love the Duo for video, but I don’t watch much video on my iPhone. I almost never watch YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram Reels. And for shows and movies, I stick with my TV screen and an Apple TV 4K.

Multitasking support on iPhone Duo works really well. But when I found myself needing to multitask, I still reached for my iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard attached. A keyboard-free product can’t replace my main computer (nor would I expect it to), and the Duo screen was too small to comfortably work on it.

Last year I bought an iPhone Air and absolutely loved it. Initially, the Air’s less capable camera system didn’t bother me, it was “good enough.”

After a few months though, I started missing the Pro camera system more. Then I learned that my wife was pregnant with twins, and I knew I wanted the best possible iPhone cameras to capture their early weeks and months. So I bought an iPhone 18 Pro in September.

I’ve been very impressed by iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera upgrades, and it’s great having a Telephoto lens again too. Since having the best camera system is so crucial for me right now, I knew iPhone Duo couldn’t be my only iPhone.

I initially planned to dual-carry the two models, using iPhone 18 Pro solely as a camera. But over and over I found myself wishing it was my only iPhone.

I returned mine as well. Beautiful device, but functionally not very good.

Is the iPhone Duo camera good enough for most people? Probably so. But for this year at least, with my twins aging rapidly, it’s not quite right for me. If I loved the Duo for other reasons, I would just use both models. But since I didn’t, I’m happy to stick with the iPhone 18 Pro.

In closing, I want to explicitly state that I don’t think the iPhone Duo is a bad product, and this isn’t a “bad review.”

The iPhone Duo just isn’t for me. I get the sense, though, that it’s lots of people’s favorite iPhone in years. Apple created its most unique new iPhone model since the original, and there’s plenty to love about it. I’m very curious to see how popular foldables become over time compared to slab models, because each clearly offers pros and cons. But for me, at least right now, the iPhone 18 Pro is my model of choice.

What has your iPhone Duo experience been like so far? Love it? Undecided? Let us know in the comments.

#3374. HBO's 9-Part Thriller Masterpiece Has Earned Its Status As A Modern Classic

There was a time when superhero TV shows were synonymous with colorful costumes, campy action, and plots that focused much more on outlandish spectacle than delivering anything grounded or relatable. The genre has, thankfully, developed a grittier and more realistic edge in the age of streaming. Modern superhero series like The Penguin, Daredevil: Born Again, and Lanterns have ditched the obsession with superpowered spectacle to instead focus on the injustices and inequality that lead to heroes taking up their mantles in the first place.

That approach to small-screen superhero stories feels familiar in the 2020s, but this definitely wasn’t always the case. The prestige superhero series model didn’t come out of nowhere, either. There’s a show that paved the way for contemporary hits that give the genre its current level of dramatic clout and mainstream respect among those who’d once never have given a superhero story a chance. That series is 2019’s Watchmen, HBO’s sequel miniseries to Alan Moore’s groundbreaking graphic novel.

Set in Tulsa 34 years after the attack on New York in Alan Moore’s original story, Watchmen introduces viewers to detective Angela Abar (Regina King) as she investigates a white supremacist group. The case draws her into the lives of the original Watchmen vigilantes while continuing the graphic novel’s questioning of whether wearing a mask and calling oneself a hero is enough to make it true. While it may not be a superhero household name, shows like The Penguin, Lanterns, and Daredevil: Born Again may not ever have existed without HBO’s Watchmen to pave the way.

While there were several grittier superhero shows arriving around the same time as Watchmen, such as The Boys in the same year or the Netflix-Marvel shows that began with Daredevil in 2015, none of them felt like they changed the game in quite the same way as HBO’s miniseries. For years, the selling points of pretty much every superhero TV show were its hero, its villain, and the prospect of seeing them fight. Watchmen bucked this trend in a way few, if any, series had before.

Rather than focusing on setting up a hero-villain showdown, HBO’s Watchmen built itself around a mystery. It didn’t feel like a superhero show. It felt like a detective show that just so happened to have superheroes in it. What’s more, these “heroes” are far from morally good. Watchmen presents its masked vigilantes not as saviors, but as ordinary people with their own ideological agendas. It’s an approach that put a fresh spin on the familiar tropes of the genre. For example, secret identities shift from being a way for heroes to protect their loved ones to a way to use anonymity to negate accountability.

Opening with the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre also gave Watchmen a sense of history and political relevance that superhero TV series rarely attempted at the time. By the time the action reaches 2019, generations have grown up with different ideas about what a hero is and who deserves their protection. Who counts as a hero and a villain depends on perspective, with those that society labels as the former often working to hold up corrupt institutions and protect a societal status quo that perpetuates inequality.

That shift from the traditional hero-vs-villain setup to a politically charged mystery narrative won Watchmen no shortage of acclaim, including 11 Primetime Emmy wins. At the time, a superhero series receiving this much critical praise was basically unheard of. It was a true turning point for the genre on the small screen. Many gritty and grounded superhero TV shows have followed in the years since, but none have made as much of an impact on the genre itself quite like Watchmen.

While Watchmen is celebrated today and was far from a ratings flop when it aired in 2019, it didn’t perform as well as it could have done given just how good it is. The reasons why are obvious, too. While it’s an incredible piece of television in its own right, early discussions about Watchmen were defined not by its merits, but by its relation to the source material. Alan Moore’s Watchmen comics are among the most beloved of all time. As is often the case with such highly regarded properties, HBO’s adaptation became defined by the divisive and often toxic responses of the existing fandom.

Even the announcement that HBO was creating a sequel to Watchmen was met with immediate and disproportionately vocal backlash. Many fans of the original graphic novel wanted Alan Moore’s story to stand alone. This wasn’t just down to longtime fans wanting the existing canon and timeline to remain untouched, either. There were also some particularly toxic and abhorrent reactions to racism becoming central to HBO’s story too. For casual viewers who weren’t at all familiar with the Watchmen comic, the discussions surrounding the 2019 miniseries made it seem like a hotbed of controversy that it simply wasn’t worth wading into.

This is an incredible shame, because Watchmen is an incredibly solid thriller that even viewers completely unaware of Alan Moore’s original graphic novel are bound to appreciate. It’s not just a game-changing superhero TV series, it’s a rich mystery story that uses its genre as a tool to explore some incredibly poignant themes and topics. While it’s impossible to say for certain, it feels likely that Watchmen would today be much more widely discussed if its legacy wasn't defined by the polarizing pop-culture discourse that surrounded it when it arrived in 2019.
